subsubtopic: JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERED DURING WORLD WAR II- NATIONAL REDRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, nearly half a century ago, in the crisis of wartime, the Government of Canada wrongfully incarcerated, seized the property, and disenfranchised thousands of citizens of Japanese ancestry. We cannot change the past. But we must, as a nation, have the courage to face up to these historical facts.
The issue of Japanese-Canadian redress is one which I raised in the House of Commons more than four years ago with the Prime Minister of the day when I was Leader of the Opposition. I said then in this House:
There is a world of difference between regret and a formal apology. Canadians of Japanese origin had their rights trampled upon. The reputation of this country was besmirched.
Since then, Mr. Speaker, the present Government has sought a settlement with the Japanese-Canadian community to put things right between them and their country; to put things right with the surviving members of the Japanese-Canadian wartime community of 22,000 persons; to put things right with their children, and ours, so that they can walk together in this country, burdened neither by the wrongs nor the grievances of previous generations.
It is fitting that representatives of the National Association of Japanese Canadians are present in the visitors' gallery on this solemn occasion because today I have the honour to announce, on behalf of the Government of Canada, that a comprehensive redress settlement has been reached with the National Association of Japanese Canadians on behalf of their community.

subsubtopic: JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERED DURING WORLD WAR II- NATIONAL REDRESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERED DURING WORLD WAR II- NATIONAL REDRESS
speechtext:
Perhaps the most important element of this redress is the official acknowledgement of the wrongs of the 1940s. But redress must go beyond words and laws-important as they are for our present understanding and our future actions. The Minister of State for Multiculturalism and
Citizenship (Mr. Weiner) will be announcing the details of the settlement, and I pay special tribute today to his skill and resolve in this matter, and to the Secretary of State (Mr. Bouchard) who, immediately after his swearing in as a Minister of the Crown, made the resolution of this important moral issue a matter of the highest priority for him and his colleagues. In a special way, I readily acknowledge the strong moral leadership on this particular question and, indeed, others, that has long been provided by the Hon. Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser), the very distinguished Speaker of the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERED DURING WORLD WAR II- NATIONAL REDRESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERED DURING WORLD WAR II- NATIONAL REDRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 think all Members of the House know that no amount of money can right the wrong, undo the harm, and heal the wounds. But it is symbolic of our determination to address this issue, not only in the moral sense but also in a tangible way. In that spirit, we will accept applications for the granting of Canadian citizenship to eligible persons of Japanese ancestry who were expelled from Canada or had their citizenship revoked during these years. We will also accept requests for the clearing of names of eligible persons of Japanese ancestry who were convicted of violations under the War Measures Act-thankfully now gone from our texts of law in Canada-and the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act.
As well, in commemoration of all who suffered these injustices, we will establish a Canadian Race Relations Foundation to foster racial harmony and cross-cultural understanding in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, not only was the treatment inflicted on Japanese-Canadians during the War both morally and legally unjustified, it went against the very nature of our country, of Canada. We are a pluralistic society. We each respect the language, opinions and religious convictions of our neighbour. We celebrate our linguistic duality and our cultural diversity. We know that the strength of our country lies in the collective energies of its regions. We are tolerant people who live in freedom in a land of abundance. That is the Canada of our ancestors. That is the Canada our ancestors worked to build. That is the kind of country we want to leave our children, the Canada of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms,

September 22, 1988
Statements by Ministers
the new Official Languages Act and the Canadian Multicul-turalism Act. A Canada that at all times and in all circumstances works hard to eliminate racial discrimination at home and abroad.

A Canada, Mr. Speaker, that is able to face up to the mistakes of the past, and so become better prepared to face the challenges of the future.
1 am tabling at this time the specific terms of the Government's historic agreement with the National Association of Japanese Canadians. 1 will meet later this morning with the President of the National Association of Japanese Canadians and some of his colleagues who are with him today to formalize this special agreement.
Most of us in our own lives have had occasion to regret certain things that we have done. Error is an ingredient of humanity, so too is apology and forgiveness. We all have learned from personal experience that as inadequate as apologies are they are the only way we can cleanse the past so that we may, as best we can, in good conscience face the future.
1 know that I speak for Members on all sides of the House today in offering to Japanese Canadians the formal and sincere apology of this Parliament for those past injustices against them, against their families, and against their heritage, and our solemn commitment and undertaking to Canadians of every origin that such violations will never again in this country be countenanced or repeated.

subsubtopic: JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERED DURING WORLD WAR II- NATIONAL REDRESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERED DURING WORLD WAR II- NATIONAL REDRESS
speechtext:
It is an honour for me to rise on behalf of my colleagues in the Liberal Party caucus in response to the very historic announcement made only moments ago by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney). My Leader finds himself in Vancouver this morning and, unfortunately, will not be in a position to respond in kind on the floor of the House of Commons. However, he will be making a statement from Vancouver on this very historic announcement later in the day.
As the Prime Minister indicated, the Minister of State for Multiculturalism and Citizenship (Mr. Weiner) will be revealing the details of this redress package later today. 1 have yet to see those details, but 1 trust that they will be in keeping with the aspirations articulated so well for so long by the National Association of Japanese Canadians, and agreeable to the Japanese Canadian citizens and residents in that very proud community.
Towards that end, I am pleased today that the federal Government and this Parliament has moved to redress the injustices that were inflicted against an important and integral part of our Canadian society, Canadian citizens who happen to be of Japanese ancestry. In doing so, it closes the chapter of what was a very sad and sensitive memory in our history.
While one's home, land, and business once lost can never be replaced, and while being evicted from one's own community and separated from one's own family and friends leaves a deep and emotional scar that can never be completely erased from the soul of those Canadian citizens, today's commitment by Government and by Parliament will serve as best as possible to heal those very deep wounds and concerns.
Moreover, today's actions are underlined by an important and symbolic message, a message of fairness and justice for all, that this nation stands for equality for all Canadians, and that there can only be, and must only be, one first-class citizenship for all Canadians.
It is with a great sense of pride and history, therefore, that I am able to speak on behalf of my Party and join the Prime Minister in issuing this most important apology to the Japanese Canadian community of Canada.
It is not a sign of weakness for a country to render this apology. Instead, it is a sure sign of strength and a sign of reflection of our country's commitment to try wherever and however to right our wrongs, not merely for the sake of correcting the history books but, more important perhaps, to establish important standards that will serve Canadians today and future generations of Canadians tomorrow. In addition, today's actions are not so much about a multicultural issue as much as about an issue of Canadian justice.
In closing, I wish to pay a special tribute and commend Mr. Art Miki, his colleagues from the National Association of Japanese Canadians, and its members and friends in the Japanese Canadian community at large, for their never ending determination and deep belief in the cause that they carried so well for so long. Today's resolution, no doubt, is a tribute to their sense of purpose, but it is also an appropriate response to those who continue to question the legitimacy and motivation of the leadership of the National Association of Japanese Canadians.
It is also fitting that the Prime Minister pointed out the pivotal role played behind the scenes by our Hon. Speaker who, to 1 can say publicly to him, offered us a sense of encouragement in the day-to-day questions that we posed on the floor of the House of Commons over the last four years. I join in saluting our Hon. Speaker, and indeed the other Members of Parliament who may not be making a statement this morning but who nevertheless played a significant role.
Finally, on this historic day, we cannot forget the many Japanese Canadians who were interned but who are no longer with us, unfortunately. Their children refuse to forget the hardships of their forefathers. It would have been my hope, indeed it would have been our collective hope, that they too could be with us today to witness and be part of the day that they had dearly longed for.
September 22, 1988

However, I say today, and I believe all Members share this, that their struggles were not in vain for their efforts kept that flame of hope alive and bright. It was the strength of that flame that provided the foundation for today's resolution. This agreement, in large part, is their agreement as well.

subsubtopic: JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERED DURING WORLD WAR II- NATIONAL REDRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great pleasure to the Prime Minister's speech today. Forty-six years ago, the Government of Canada took measures against Japanese-Canadians that were unjust and unacceptable. Today, at last, we have started to make amends.

In the 1940s our Government, a democratically elected Government, did a great injustice to some 22,000 of our citizens, a permanent injustice to those who are no longer living. This was done, not because of what they had done, but because of who they were. These Japanese Canadians had their families broken up, their property confiscated, their businesses destroyed. They were forced to abandon their homes on the coast of British Columbia and they were forced to move to the interior and to elsewhere in Canada.
They, as Canadian citizens, had done no wrong. They were the victims of intolerance and racism brought about, not because we were at war with them but because we were at war with the land of their ancestors. They had done no wrong to any of their fellow citizens. It was an inglorious moment in our, on the whole, proud history.
Today we are formally acknowledging this wrong, and I am pleased that today's representatives of Canadians of Japanese ancestry have been able to reach an agreement with the Government of Canada. On behalf of all members of my Party and, I am sure in a sense I speak for everyone in the House of Commons and Canadians wherever they may live, I bid a special welcome to those Canadians of Japanese ancestry who are with us today in the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERED DURING WORLD WAR II- NATIONAL REDRESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERED DURING WORLD WAR II- NATIONAL REDRESS
speechtext:
I would like to stress that when we talk about the grievous injustice that was inflicted, we are not talking about an abstract breaking of an abstract right. We are talking about profound, serious human suffering. As an example, 1 would like to cite a quotation from an extremely moving Canadian novel by a Canadian of Japanese ancestry. It is called Obasan, and it is written by Joy Kogawa. It is a story of the life experience of families at this time. It is noted that the families are fictional but all experiences are very real. At one point the heroine of the novel, who is in her thirties,
Statements by Ministers
describes the impact this has had on her life. I know it is a true story. She says:
The fact is I never got used to it and I cannot, I cannot bear the memory. There are some nightmares from which there is no waking, only deeper and deeper sleep.
There is a word for it. Hardship. The hardship is so pervasive, so inescapable, so thorough, it's a noose around my chest and I cannot move anymore.
1 repeat, Mr. Speaker, these have been real experiences in real lives for which our parliamentary ancestors have to assume responsibility because they made those decisions that led to that experience. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has said, we all make errors. Our predecessors in this great Chamber of ours made errors. One of the important and fundamental ways of addressing these errors is at least to apologize publicly and acknowledge the serious wrong that was done, and that we are doing. However, in so doing, we must keep in mind that it does not mitigate at all the horrible experience that has been inflicted upon those victims.
The Prime Minister quite appropriately alluded to the work that has been done by present generations in redressing this wrong here in the House. I think it might have been appropriate to cite those people who stood up at the time because they were present. They were Canadians who said it was wrong, who went against the force of public opinion, who fought for civil liberties at a time when it was important to do the fighting and not talk about redressing wrongs that were done by others. It is easy for us in one sense, although appropriate, to do that. I would like to cite a few words of a distinguished Member of Parliament at that time. He had this to say, clearly in the face of public opinion:
If we are to have harmonious and friendly relations between the oriental population and the rest of our British Columbia citizens, we must stop discriminating against and abusing the orientals. We must find some common ground on which we can work, and I think it can be found ... I am satisfied that if we treat the Japanese and our other oriental citizens right, we shall get their loyalty,.. .
He went on to say:
I know them, speak to them; I visit them and have them in my home, and I have not the slightest doubt that what I say is correct. If we are to avoid the troubles that other countries have had with racial minorities, then we must take a realistic view of the situation in British Columbia and attempt to make these people feel at home among us. We will secure their loyalty by fairness and kindness and by the practice of those other attributes which we exercise in our relations with other people.
He was speaking of fellow Canadians citizens. That speech was given in this House on February 25, 1941, by Angus Maclnnis, the then Member for Vancouver-Kingsway.
I want simply to conclude by complimenting the Government of the day on behalf of my Party in reaching this agreement and by saying, as one politician: 1 hope this kind of experience for us as a nation will never ever be repeated.

subsubtopic: TRANSPORT ACROSS METROPOLITAN TORONTO-REPORT OF TASK FORCE-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, i have the pleasure to table, in both official languages, the final report of the Toronto Area Rail Transportation of Dangerous Goods Task Force.
This report was commissioned by the Government in March, 1986, to investigate the feasibility of rerouting or relocating the movement of dangerous goods around Metropolitan Toronto. The task force was also requested to investigate and make recommendations on the relationship between train speed and safety.
This report finds rail movement of dangerous goods in Metro Toronto safe, not only related to other modes but compared to other countries as well. CP Rail is the safest railway in North America; CN currently ranks fifth. This is a tribute, not only to the employees of each railway but also to the commitment the Government has to ensuring safe transportation systems for all Canadians.
When I received the report last night from task force Chairman Harold Gilbert, we had the opportunity to discuss its consultations, findings, and recommendations.

Although the task force submitted 130 recommendations, my comments today will be limited to the two most important aspects of its mandate: train speed and rerouting of traffic.
The task force asked a consulting firm to investigate the relationship between train speed and safety. Although the report is technical in nature, it implies that from the safety point of view, speed reduction might not be necessary. The task force recommends further studies in this area.

I have considered carefully the representations made by citizens, municipal Governments, and Members of this House. Further, I note that three members of the task force expressed the view that lower speed limits were desirable on the tracks identified as high risk.
I have considered these matters in light of my primary concern, which is safety. I think that the best course is to lower the speed limits on the high-risk routes. I shall immediately take the necessary steps to set and enforce the lower speed limits on the following rail lines: from Weston Road on Canadian National's Weston Subdivision and from Starview Drive on the Canadian Pacific's McTier Subdivision to the West Toronto Diamond, from Kipling Avenue on Canadian Pacific's Galt Subdivision to the West Toronto Diamond, from the West Toronto Diamond along the Canadian Pacific's North Toronto Subdivision to their Agincourt Yard in Scarborough, and from Canadian National's McMillan Yard along their York Subdivision eastward to Doncaster.
The task force recommends that all levels of Government collaborate in approaching the issues of rerouting and relocation. The task force does not see this as an issue solely of safety. It states that relocation has an economic effect, and it has a primary effect on land use and zoning policies on the provincial and municipal Governments.
I could not agree more, and since this is a matter of provincial jurisdiction 1 would like to inform Hon. Members that I will be writing today to the Hon. Ed Fulton, Ontario Minister of Transportation, seeking the province's position.

During the last four years, the Government's commitment to safety has lead to a number of initiatives, including the regulations on the transportation of hazardous materials, adopted in 1985; the Railway Safety Act, which received Royal Assent on July 28 this year; and the Bill to establish the Transportation Accident Investigation Board, tabled in the House not long ago.

The Standing Committee on Transport has played a vital role in all these matters, many of which bear on the task force's recommendations. With its knowledge, expertise, and accessibility to the public and industry, I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the standing committee can best advance the work of the task force. Therefore, 1 am referring this report to the standing committee.
The report 1 have received includes all public submissions made to the task force. I shall provide these to the standing committee along with a minority report prepared by a member of the task force. As well, 1 would advise the House that the report of the Vancouver Task Force on Dangerous Goods is expected to be completed in the next few weeks. It is my intention to refer that report to the standing committee.
I would like to take this opportunity to thank Harold Gilbert for his excellent work and dedication to this project. This has been a very intensive and demanding study, and all task force members are to be congratulated for their commitment of time and expertise.

subsubtopic: TRANSPORT ACROSS METROPOLITAN TORONTO-REPORT OF TASK FORCE-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we received the report today with a sense of happiness because the process has been completed. Having listened to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard), 1 think there are a few remarks that have to be made from this side of the House.
The report is finished. The process was a lengthy one but was very thorough. It had to delve into very complex and difficult issues. Out of that process, 130 recommendations have emerged. Now the Minister must act. We have mixed feelings because this report is vague and in some respects requires further studies. Here is where the political crunch comes. The Minister of Transport must make certain difficult decisions very soon because the process has now come to an end and further studies are not desirable.
September 22, 1988

It is curious that out of 130 recommendations the Minister has pulled out two to comment upon today. They are, of course, very political and very urgent. These are issues which have been the object of engagement, attention, and battles by individuals and organizations in Metro Toronto over several years in this decade. They have initiated this process and participated in it. 1 refer in particular to the Metro-Toronto Residents' Action Committee.
The question of speed leaves a lot to be desired in this report. It is true that on page 61 the report focuses on the importance of looking at other factors and urges that attention be given to addressing and removing, on an utmost priority basis, the track, equipment, operational, and track defect causes of accidents. That is good stuff and we concur with that. Those would be, in other words, preventive measures and good and intensive maintenance for every train entering the Metro Toronto area. I suppose that applies to any urban centre across the country.
We agree with that, but why has the speed limit not been spelled out, both in the report and in the statement by the Minister here today? They only refer to lower speed limits, leaving us, the organizations, and the citizens in the dark as to what the speed limit will be. Will it be one kilometer per hour, or will it be 30 kilometers per hour? Will it be 40 kilometers per hour, as suggested by M-TRAC in a number of submissions even before this commission, or is the Minister's limit a faster one? In other words, this vague commitment is not enough and it is not worth very much.
Let me deal with relocation. In this case we see the Meech Lake values emerging again. The Minister will write a letter to the Minister of Transport of the province today, and that is all. The Minister said in his statement that transportation of this kind and relocation has an economic effect and a primary effect on land use and zoning policies of the provincial and municipal Governments. What about the federal Government? Does the federal Government not exist as well? Does it not have an interest as well in this debate and therefore require the leadership of the Minister of Transport of the day rather than a letter to the Minister of Transport of the Province of Ontario? That is not good enough.
I doubt very much that Toronto residents will sleep any easier because the Minister has written a letter. It is a pathetic response to such an important issue that affects millions of people in the Metropolitan Toronto area.
Instead, the Minister should convene a meeting and discuss this with his provincial colleague and municipal authorities in such a fashion as to take leadership on a very complex matter. Canadian National and Canadian Pacific would not have been built if the attitude of the Government of the day were such as the Minister put forward today in the House, saying that it is a provincial and municipal responsibility. It is a federal responsibility as well.
Statements by Ministers
I referred to M-TRAC for a very good reason. It has long been involved in the issue of transportation of dangerous goods. In a way, this report is a result of the efforts of the citizens' organization. These efforts have been persistent and have made the question of public safety the first priority in the transportation of dangerous goods. Progress has been made over the years as a result of that.
Of the recommendations that M-TRAC has made, four were ignored. One recommendation is to treat empty railcars that have carried dangerous goods as full for the purposes of safety restrictions. That has not been dealt with yet.
The second recommendation was to limit the number of hazardous goods cars to 20 per train. I know that the report takes a different position on that, but it remains extremely vague as to what is the optimal length of trains transporting dangerous goods. Again, the Minister must give leadership on this question and come up with an answer that will strike a balance that will give priority to safety.
The third recommendation was that the length of trains with hazardous goods cars that are full should be limited. The report does not seem to deal with this question. The recommendation was that it should not be longer than 1,600 metres, which is more than one and a half kilometers.
Finally, the recommendation to ensure that there are enough inspectors to monitor and enforce safety standards is a crucial issue. It is a preventive measure and a recommendation I would particularly stress to the Minister so that he has in his budget the means to hire the inspectors for trains entering metropolitan areas across the nation. That is where the entrance of the train becomes crucial. That is partially dealt with, although not in a conclusive manner, when talking about train gateways inspections at page 58. However, we must ask whether the inspectors are there and whether the number is adequate. Is the quality of the inspection sufficient?
In conclusion, the Minister has only addressed the first two of many issues. The speed of trains remains unclear. 1 hope the Minister will soon make a statement as to the speed he envisages when talking about lower speed.
We want the Minister to address the other substantive issues in this report, in particular, the issue that M-TRAC has persistently raised over the years and which, in a way, triggered the process that led to the writing and tabling of this report today.

subsubtopic: TRANSPORT ACROSS METROPOLITAN TORONTO-REPORT OF TASK FORCE-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course I have not had time to examine the report. I will keep my remarks general in nature and begin by saying that railways are still the safest form of transport for the handling of dangerous goods.
I know that railways receive many headlines and much coverage when there is a train mishap because it is more spectacular. There is little or no reporting and little public knowledge about the thousands of mishaps in the trucking industry that occur on our highways every year.

September 22, 1988
Statements by Ministers
I suggest to the Minister and the Government that the continued acceptance of rail line abandonment means an ever greater shift of the amounts of traffic of dangerous goods to our already congested urban streets and main highways.
Both railways want to abandon another 15,000 miles of track over the next seven years. They have already abandoned several thousand miles of track in western Canada. Now it is occurring in central and eastern Canada. Would you believe, Mr. Speaker, that one of the railways wants to abandon the line from Montreal to North Bay through Ottawa?
The continuing trend to allow the elimination of siding and spur tracks in our industrial and warehouse areas in cities all over Canada, not only Toronto, increases the concentration of truck movement of all those commodities, including dangerous goods, on our urban roads system and our main highways. That increases the number of accidents and risks involving trucks.
Many people may not realize in our society that thousands of truckloads or partial truckloads of dangerous commodities move on our streets every day out of sheer necessity. Trucks haul explosives like gunpowder and ammunition to hardware stores. They haul various kinds of solvents and cleaning fluids to stores all over our cities. This occurs every day with thousands of vehicles everywhere in Canada. Let us not delude ourselves into thinking that by doing something about the movement of dangerous goods on railways through our urban centres we will suddenly reduce the risk. Frankly, I do not think it will.
We can handle much of this with present infrastructure along with some modifications, better operating rules, a better system of inspection and better enforcement by the Government of Canada over the maintenance of railway rolling stock and all transportation vehicles, including the trucking industry. [DOT]
[DOT] (M50)
When one sees the railroads reducing their track forces, reducing the number of inspectors and carmen they have at many locations across Canada, one would think that the Government and the National Transportation Agency would show some alarm. But it is always the bottom-line syndrome that takes over. The trucking industry is in regulatory shambles. We were promised, with the introduction of Bill C-19, that there would be an agreement reached among the 13 jurisdictions-the two Territories, the 10 provinces and the federal Government-on a standardized regulatory regime across Canada, whether it was with respect to licensing, load limits, speed limits, handling of dangerous goods, or whatever. The agreement still has not been arrived at. In that respect one of my colleagues mentioned the Meech Lake Accord again.
The federal Government has complete and total jurisdiction and legal authority, constitutional authority, on all trucking
that moves inter-provincially and internationally. If the provinces do not want to or refuse to co-operate with respect to a standard set of rules, regulations and practices, then it seems to me that the federal Government must exercise its responsibility and do it.
I want to mention another item about the whole matter of safety. I want you, Mr. Speaker, to visualize something that has occurred and can occur again. In Canada there are thousands and thousands of vehicles carrying dangerous goods which travel our roads and which go over something in the order of 100,000 level crossings. If a locomotive hits one of those vehicles on the Prairies-the thousands of farm fuel vehicles-travelling over all our roads, or in the cities, and a truck bursts into flames with an entire crew in the locomotive, and with them are all the documents that say what are the contents of that train, including which cars have dangerous goods and what kind of dangerous goods, and that locomotive also bursts into flames, who is going to notify whom about what? There is nobody in the caboose because there is no caboose to put up a phone and call the fire department, the police and the ambulances, and to notify the nearest Dangerous Goods Directorate. Mr. Speaker, they would not listen, and the Government has authorized this high risk and unsafe practice.
I want to say one final thing, Mr. Speaker, about rail line relocation, which is fine when you get it in the right location. My own City of Regina is a classic case of approval being given by Government to relocate track and rail yards in the wrong place, and at a cost beyond the financial capacity of the city. 1 hope the Minister will review and overturn the CTC decision and make that city and the railroads go back to the drawing board. Unless there is a fully informed and consulted public on rail line relocation, then the NIMBY, "not in my back yard", syndrome takes over, similar to what happens with waste disposal sites.
I think the standing committee will welcome the opportunity to deal with the report. I hope it will deal with it with relative speed and hear from people right across Canada. I hope that there will not be any question about the committee being provided with the fullest resources, both financially and staffwise, as well as reasonable time to do a thorough job.
Something that the Minister might wish to consider when he is looking over the Toronto situation, but something which also concerns Thunder Bay, Windsor and Vancouver as well as a lot of other locations, is one wide multi-track corridor with both railroads being required to use it as a possible solution. I think that in many locations in the country this is something that could be looked at which would probably in the long run be cheaper to put in and to keep operating.
September 22, 1988

subsubtopic: CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my honour to present a petition pursuant to Standing Order 106 on behalf of a number of constituents from western Canada who believe that the present Government lacks a mandate from the people of Canada to conclude a trade deal with the United States.
They believe very strongly, Mr. Speaker, that as a result of the trade deal Canadian sovereignty would be seriously compromised. They believe also that the deal itself would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine its own economic future and undermine Canada's ability to build a society distinct from that of the United States.
They actually have a whole number of other concerns. Let me simply summarize by saying that they are asking for Parliament to dissolve now to allow the people of Canada an opportunity to accept or reject the proposed trade deal during a national general election.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION
speechtext:
1. No. Providing postal services through a "franchised" outlet is a relatively new approach for the Corporation. A "postal franchise" has never existed at the Lake Bonavista Shopping Centre. However, until recently there was a private sector postal outlet located in the Shopping Centre-known as a Retail Postal Outlet.
In the immediate vicinity of Lake Bonavista Shopping Centre, there are two Retail Postal Outlets currently operating. These include RPO No. 122 in Southcentre Mall, located at Macleod Trail and Anderson Road, and RPO No. 156 in the Deer Valley Shopping Centre, located at Canyon Meadows Drive and Bow Bottom Trail.

September 22, 1988
Orders for Return
The Southcentre Mall and the Deer Valley Shopping Centre have been identified as future full service sites, which will improve the accessibility of products and services in the immediate area. Currently, customers must travel approximately 2.5 km from the Lake Bonavista Shopping Centre, to Postal Station "F" for full service.
In addition to these two full service sites, there will be approximately 12 stamp shops in the area, including one at the Lake Bonavista Shopping Centre.
In keeping with Canada Post Corporation's commitment to providing improved customer access to postal products and services, this new configuration of postal outlets means better service for residents in the Lake Bonavista area.
(a)	The Lake Bonavista Shopping Centre Retail Postal Outlet (formerly known as a sub-post office) was in operation for more than a decade, until its recent closure by the operator in early 1988.
(b)	Financial arrangements between Canada Post Corporation and its private sector operators is considered proprietary information. The outlet located at the Shopping Centre was a private sector outlet and, therefore, the operator's remuneration was based on revenues at the outlet.

Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of State and Minister of State
(Treasury Board)): Mr. Speaker, I move:
September 22, 1988

That, in relation to Bill C-144, an Act to authorize payments by Canada toward the provision of child care services, and to amend the Canada Assistance Plan in consequence thereof, not more than one further sitting day be allotted to the third reading stage of the Bill; and
That fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for government business on the day allotted to the consideration of the third reading stage of the said Bill, any proceedings before the House shall be interrupted, if required, for the purpose of this Order and, in turn, every question necessary in order to dispose of the stage of the Bill then under consideration shall be put forthwith and successively, without further debate or amendment.
I should not take too long in my remarks in this debate. We have brought forward, I believe, historic, innovative social legislation which, for the first time in Canada, will set up a child care system. It is very much in keeping with the direction of this Government to give people a hand up and not a hand out.
It is innovative in that it has various ways of applying the funding. I appreciate that some will say that it is not enough and others will say that it should be done differently, but we think we have a good start on this social legislation and we want to implement it. We want to proceed as quickly as we can to get this to the Senate, in the hopes that the Senate will move quickly on this legislation.
We have suffered a delay on the Bill at other stages of debate. I am speaking of the days when it was called at second reading, where we considered the Bill in principle.
I would draw to the House's attention the remarks of my friend from Kamloops-Shuswap, who said, as reported on page 19481 of yesterday's Hansard'.
I do nol see any reason for wanting to rush this legislation through. We will debate for the rest of the week, all of next week and the following weeks, until it is appropriately debated.
I find that unfortunate. It indicates that my colleague from Kamloops-Shuswap has no care or feeling for the children of this country or for single parents or for parents who work. I know that that Party makes a great to do about looking after ordinary Canadians, but with that one statement my friend has abandoned Canadians with children and Canadian children. I am not sure whether that is now NDP policy or whether he will wish to retract it in his remarks. I would hope that he would, because I know him to be a caring person, and I find that remark to be completely out of character with his normal conduct. Hopefully, during his comments he will retract that.
I do not need to spend any more time on my feet than is necessary. I would say this to the Opposition, that it would be our intention to call this on Monday, and if my friend wants to sit through lunch on Monday and get an extra hour's debate in, we would be amenable to that. We do intend that the Bill will be called Monday, that the debate at third reading will be wrapped up, and this important piece of legislation will be sent to the Senate.
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, we have here another example of the most hypocritical, double-talking Government in recent history. On the one hand we have a Government which continually talks about parliamentary reform, parliamentary democracy, but on the other hand the same Government has used closure more
Time Allocation
than any other Government in Canadian history. It has used closure and allocation of time to crush debate in this House of Commons more than any other Government. But they are talking out of both sides of their mouth. One minute it is "what a great job we are doing to enhance parliamentary reform and parliamentary democracy", but in Bill after Bill they crush the debate, close off debate, before there is a chance for the debate really to get under way.
In this case, the Minister of State introduced a motion for allocation of time, a motion to close debate for third reading, after only three Members had spoken in this House.
The only people who had spoken were the Minister for National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), who introduced the debate on third reading, then the critic for the Liberal Party, then the critic for the New Democratic Party, and right away the Minister introduced a motion to close the debate.
Once again, the Government, with its large majority, the largest parliamentary majority in Canadian history, is using that majority to crush parliamentary debate in Canada and to stop a discussion on what is one of the most complex and controversial Bills to come before this Parliament in this session.
What is the history of this Bill? The Government promised legislation on day care in the all-Party debate during the election of 1984. It was in the summer of 1984 that this Government promised new legislation on child care. Yet, we only got the Bill on July 25, 1988. We only got the Bill this summer, in a situation where the Government moved that the House sit all summer, because it could not manage its own legislative program. It decided to introduce the Bill on July 25, 1988. The Government is now accusing the Opposition of delaying.
If this Bill is not passed prior to an expected fall election, then surely the fault is not with the Opposition. The fault is surely not with the Senate. The Bill has not even been sent to the Senate yet. The fault is with the Government. It is the Government that delayed the Bill from 1984 until July 25, 1988.
There has not been a filibuster on this Bill. How can the Government say that there has been delay on this Bill when it introduced the motion, when all we had was the Minister and the chief opposition critic speaking?
On second reading, we only had three days of debate. In the legislative committee on this Bill, a very complex and controversial Bill, as I said, we only had three and a third days of discussion and hearings, despite a demand by groups from all over the country that they be heard on this Bill and be given adequate time to be heard.
On report stage, we only had two days, because Your Honour had ruled out of order many of the amendments that had been proposed. We are at third reading and the Government has just put a motion that we limit debate to one more day.

September 22, 1988
Time Allocation
This attempt by the Government to limit debate on this very complex and controversial Bill is totally, totally unacceptable. 1 want to point out, so that Canadians will know, that in the three and a third days of committee hearings the Government again used its majority to force all the witnesses to be heard in those three and a third days. There were 40 groups that came before the committee to be heard and the Government gave each one of those groups a half an hour or less. Can you imagine, anyone with any experience in Parliament saying to a group that might come from Montreal, Vancouver or the Atlantic provinces, "We want to hear you but you only have 30 minutes to make your presentation and answer questions from members of the committee"? What nonsense. Usually we give the witness groups at least one hour in committee.
These witnesses and members of the committee were forced to deal with this Bill in just half an hour. 1 say forced, because a motion was passed by Conservative Members cutting off debate in committee, forcing 40 groups to make their presentations within that very short period of time, and all in Ottawa. The committee did not seek opinions outside Ottawa. The groups had to come to Ottawa.
This Bill is supposed to be so good, but what was the unanimous opinion of those groups? Of those 40 groups that received very short hearings before the committee, not one supported the Bill. The Government could not find one group to appear before the committee to support the Bill. The only witness who supported the Bill was the Minister who is sponsoring the Bill.
Forty of the groups in Canada interested in child care came to the committee and said that the Bill was not adequate, that it does not fulfil the needs of Canadian children. Some of them even suggested that the Bill was a step backward, a regression over what we already have. They criticized this Bill first because it has no national standards. It provides money for day care, but there are no standards as to how the provinces, the municipalities and the various groups must perform in providing day care.
The Bill does not meet the needs of Canadian children. There is no provision at all for latchkey children, young children who must come home after school without parents to take care of them. It only provides for 200,000 new day care spaces over seven years. The need right now is for two million day care spaces, due to the fact that there have been radical changes in society, starting in the sixties, with more and more single mothers, more and more mothers working because of the attitudinal changes in society and the need for both father and mother to work because there is not adequate income with only one parent working to cover the housing, food, clothing and educational needs of the family.
This is a controversial, complex Bill. It was opposed by every day care group that appeared in the very short and compressed time before the committee. More debate and more hearings
are needed in order to clarify the weaknesses and shortcomings of the Bill and in order to put before the Canadian people the various alternatives on day care.
The Government has a false idea of the role of Parliament. The Government feels that because it has a majority in Parliament, the outcome of a vote is a foregone conclusion. Unfortunately, that is so. We know there are very few independent-thinking Members of Parliament on the Conservative side who will break ranks from time to time on a question of conscience. They will vote in a bloc and defeat the positions of the two opposition Parties.
We know we will be defeated on every vote put to the House, but the purpose of debate, I repeat again and again, is unfortunately not simply to convince Members on the government side. We know we will not convince them. The purpose of the debate in this House is to send arguments on different issues out of the House so the Canadian population can understand the issues. That is why the debates of this House are televised. That is why the proceedings are reported in Hansard. That is why we have a Press Gallery.
We do not expect to convince those stone-age Tories over there. By having a reasonable debate, we want to let Canadians understand the issues behind the Bill. It is a travesty of parliamentary democracy and justice that the Government should give only one more day to this debate on third reading.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-144
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you may have noted that it is dull in the House of Commons. A cloud hangs over the House of Commons once again, the cloud of closure, the cloud of a Government that has betrayed the principles of parliamentary democracy as we have come to know it in Canada.
This is a closure-crazed Government. There has never been a Government in the history of Canada that has so repeatedly decided to muzzle Parliamentarians, those who are elected to represent the people of Canada. As a matter of fact, I remember the day when Conservative Members of the House rushed the Speaker's chair and stopped the House of Commons from performing. I remember other days when, through a misuse of parliamentary tactics, Conservative Members closed down the House of Commons for day after day. The one place where Canadians could speak their minds without fear of reprisal was taken away from them. Those who were elected to represent the people of Canada had no opportunity to express the views of their constituents.
September 22, 1988

Once again, on one of the most important social issues that has faced this House of Commons in the last four years, the Government has decided not to tolerate any more discussion. As my hon. friend who just spoke indicated, the importance of this discussion is not to try to convince the parliamentary eunuchs across the way, and I call them parliamentary eunuchs because they have no power, they have no influence. Their voices are worthless.
What we are really seeing is the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) deciding that now is the time to jam, to rush, to push this legislation through the House of Commons, and he does not want to hear anybody on the government side speaking on the most important social issue to face us. That is why I call all of those Members across the way government eunuchs. They have no life, no voice, no muscle. We do not hear them represent their constituents.
I would think that there should be a revolt on the backbenches of the Government. Surely to goodness there is someone over there who believes that this is not good legislation. When this was before committee, the Conservative, Liberal and New Democrat members of the committee wanted to have experts come before us. We wanted to bring in the best the country has to offer to advise us on child care, and they came. Not many were allowed to come, because government Members wanted to rush this through the committee in only two days of committee debate.
We brought before us a whole set of witnesses, 40 different witnesses, the best and most expert voices on child care in the country. Do you know what every single witness said, Mr. Speaker? They all said we should tear up the legislation, send it back, throw it out, not proceed with it. This legislation is wrong-headed, this legislation is anti-children.
Where are the compassionate people on the government benches? Are there any? All I hear is sheep-like sounds, just "Baa, baa, baa, tell us what to do, we will cheer, we will clap like seals if that is what we have to do. We are not going to speak out on behalf of our constituents, we are not going to listen to the experts on child care".
This is not democracy. This is a dictatorship. This is dictatorial. The Prime Minister says, no more debate, no more discussion, ignore all of the expert advice on this issue and ram the legislation through. The Government has the numbers to do that, but it abuses the very principles that Canadians hold so dear, the principles of democracy and of open and free debate.
We feel very strongly about this legislation. We think this legislation should be sent back to the drawing-board and drafted properly because it was a rush job. More than four years ago, the Prime Minister said that he had as a priority the introduction of decent child care in Canada. Then 1984 went by, 1985 went by, 1986 went by, 1987 went by and 1988 nearly went by. Then, in the dying moments of this Parliament, the Prime Minister rushes in and says, "Oh, we have to
Time Allocation
jam some kind of child care legislation through the House of Commons with no decent debate, no decent examination of the legislation". Just get something through because I promised it a little over four years ago. We are dealing with legislation that makes no sense in meeting the really serious needs in Canada.
There are two million children in Canada today, Mr. Speaker, who require quality child care of one kind or another. This legislation before us is providing 200,000 child care spaces over the next seven years to meet an immediate two million space requirements. The situation will have doubled at the end of seven years in terms of need. If the Government of Canada did absolutely nothing, took the legislation and put it in a drawer or threw it away, we would be better off because in several years from now we would have more child care spaces than this legislation will provide. That is why we say it is regressive and bad legislation. It is worsening the situation from the status quo.
It is important that the people of Canada hear about this, and the only way they will be able to evaluate the situation is to hear two sides of the debate. He should provide an opportunity for opposition Members to voice their concerns and then hear from government Members why they think this is good legislation. But to do that, Mr. Speaker, you have to have a debate in the House of Commons on the most important social legislation the Government has introduced. Are we having that important debate? No, we are absolutely not. The Government has decided after one speech from each of the three political Parties-there are 282 Members of Parliament-that enough is enough. The Government has said: "We are cutting off debate and muzzling Parliamentarians, but we will set aside one more day". Can you imagine one more day of debate on the most important social legislation introduced in this House in years and years?
But that is the kind of view that presumably the Prime Minister has of democracy. 1 am not criticizing my friends opposite. I do call them political and parliamentary eunuchs. I say that because I really do not believe that they can sit there hour after hour and say nothing on this important issue. Yet they are not going to be given that opportunity, thanks to our Prime Minister.
It is undemocratic that this Bill is being rushed through. It is unparliamentary that we are jamming legislation through the House of Commons, using parliamentary Rambo-like tactics to close off debate. People say they keep hearing the distant echo of jackboots time and time again as closure is introduced this week, closure next week and closure again. There is not a Government in the history of this country that has used closure of one form or another more than this Government has.

September 22, 1988
Time Allocation
What does that tell us about the Government? Does it tell us that this Government believes in open, free debate? Of course not. It tells us that this Government does not believe in the most fundamental principles of free speech where those who are duly elected to serve Canadians in the House of Commons have an opportunity to express the views of their constituents. But we are being denied that opportunity. We are having that fundamental responsibility of Parliamentarians to reflect the views of our constituents taken away. We have been trying to reflect the views of the experts from all of the child care groups, the coalitions and the individuals who are respected from one side of Canada to another. They came to the committee and said: "Please, Mr. Prime Minister, start again. Please, Mr. Minister, don't proceed with this backward, regressive legislation. Put the interest of Canada's young people foremost rather than your political interest in terms of jamming some legislation through in the moments before an election call".
1 say this is not only a dark day for Parliament but, worse, it is a dark day for the children of Canada that we have a Government that is so uncaring, so callous, so crass in its political efforts that it is prepared to set aside the interests of Canada's young people in order to play a political agenda at the expense of the young people of Canada.

What do they agree on, Mr. Speaker? They agree that children need better quality care. They agree that our children are a tremendous asset to this nation.
What is this Parliament asked to agree on in this piece of legislation? The New Democratic Party Member who just spoke said it is regressive legislation. I will tell you what he believes is regressive, Sir. It is regressive to put more money into child care. That is his view.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-144
speechtext: That is dishonest and you know it. You are twisting the facts again.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-144
speechtext:
This is an absurd point of view from my perspective, but that is the view. This legislation is categorized
as regressive because we are putting more money into child care. That is a regressive step from a regressive Party which has a regressive view of this country.
What is the next principle in the Bill which the New Democratic Party and the Official Opposition find regressive? That parents should have a choice on how to take care of their children, that parental choice lies at the heart of the policy of our Party and at the heart of this legislation. The opposition Parties say that this is regressive, that more money is regressive, and that it is regressive that parents should have a choice about their own children.
What is the third principle involved in this Bill? That the federal Government respects the rights and the constitutional jurisdiction of the provinces. We hear that that is regressive, that it is regressive that we should have a nation in which there is co-operation between the federal Government and the provincial Governments in the provision of social services. That is not surprising for any of us who sat in this House under the last Government from 1980 to 1984. That Government cared not one whit. It was a Liberal Government which was supported by the New Democratic Party far too often. It cared not one whit for the constitutional arrangements of this country and jurisdiction. Give them half an inch and both Parties would take over education, health care, and the courts in this country. It is also consistent with their philosophy. They want to run the world and forget about provincial voters and provincial Governments.
They say the federal Government can run everything. My experience tells me that is not correct. Decisions made in Ottawa that affect the people in Trochu, Alberta are quite often not very sensitively done. When we are talking about the parents of this nation and their children, we should not have a group of elected politicians in Ottawa or bureaucrats who live in Ottawa telling the people in Newfoundland how to raise their kids. That is really what they are after. The only reason they believe this Bill is regressive is because it does not give central control about how parents should deal with their children. That is what they want, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-144
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on the Government's motion to limit the debate on Bill C-144.
I think it is the height of hypocrisy for this Government to tell Canadians that it is so concerned about day care, and then turn around and say it is not interested in hearing the views of their elected representatives.
Mr. Speaker, in fact it has acknowledged its incompetence in this area by letting Members like the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) speak to the Bill. He talked about everything except the Bill and why it was necessary to discuss it in the House. He did not explain why the Government is imposing closure. He did not explain why this Government wants to rush the Bill through the House. He did none of these things. He simply talked about matters that had no connection whatsoever with the business before the House.

We have before us a motion to limit debate. It is true, as previous speakers have said, that this Government has used time allocation, limitation, and closure more than any other Government. It has a massive majority in this House, yet it cannot control the agenda, or make up its mind so that we can come to terms with the work.
The Government brought in this bill on July 25. 1 will go through the chronology of how the Bill went through the House. On July 25, 1988, first reading of the Bill; on second reading three days of debate on August 11, 17, and 23. Government Members are the ones who called Orders of the Day. They are the ones responsible for waiting, waffling, and for not being able to make up their minds on this issue. They come in here in August and put in three days of debate.

September 22, 1988
Time Allocation
There were 11 Conservative back-benchers, including the Minister speaking on this Bill at second reading, and there were six Liberal Members, and six New Democratic Members. Is that a filibuster on second reading? No. This Bill was flawed and the Government knows it. We tried to correct it in committee. There were 40 witnesses who were given half an hour to present their points and arguments to improve the Bill. It was railroaded. There were three and a half days in committee from August 24 on. The Bill was reported back to the House on September 15. There were 13 amendments ruled in order. There was one amendment accepted by the Government. On September 22, two days ago, we started third reading of the Bill, which is the last phase of any legislative process. There was one speaker from each Party, then the Government rose and gave notice that it will invoke Standing Order 117, and limit debate to one additional day.
Yet government Members have the gall to rise today and call this a filibuster. I hope that the Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) will grow and mature a little before he uses the type of silly arguments that he was using this morning. Regressive legislation; indeed it is regressive legislation, distorted legislation, unresponsive.
Come the next election 1 hope the Member for Calgary West will self-destruct with the nonsense he has put to us today. The arguments he put were as silly as 1 have ever heard. He said that the Senate will filibuster and block the Bill. The Senate said no such thing. The Senate has not had the Bill yet, it is still here, so it cannot possibly know when it will get the Bill, unless the Government has decided once and for all to bully and bulldoze its way through and get the Bill to the Senate next week sometime. Until the Bill is there, how can the Government tell the media that it is filibustering and that it will block the Bill? 1 suspect that the least the Senate would want to do is to spend as much time as the House of Commons has, that is, three days at second reading and possibly some good committee work where they would hear these 40 witnesses who were against the Bill. There was not one witness before the committee who was in favour of the Bill, not one.

make a reasonably good argument in favour of the Bill, except for the Minister who is trying to bootleg this Bill through the House so that he can get out there and snap his suspenders or whatever they do in trying to mislead Canadians into thinking this is a good Bill. In Ontario it will be absolutely impossible for the Government to meet its requirements. The Government of Ontario had planned to expand by 12,000 spaces, but with this Government's legislative capping it at 200,000 spaces, Ontario will not be able to do it. Ontario has already announced that its expansion plans have been cut because the federal Government is refusing to fund its share over and above what Bill C-144 allows. If one looks back over the previous years, one can see a doubling, a quadrupling of spaces under the CAP program, but CAP, the Canada Assistance Program, will not work any more because it has been taken out. This Government has delayed continuously. It has not wanted to accept its responsibilities. Yet when it gets an idea, and in this case a bad idea, it bulldozes. I want to say a few things about my own preoccupation with my riding.
[ Translation]

September 22, 1988

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not a happy occasion to have to stand and speak again on a closure motion in this House. I represent the constituency of Prince Albert. That was the seat in this House represented by the Right Honourable John George Diefenbaker for 26 years. I can just imagine what that Hon. Member of Parliament would say if he were here today and saw what his colleagues, the people in his Party, are doing to Parliament. John George Diefenbaker loved this Parliament. He believed that this Parliament was the epitome of democracy and that how it operated was important to the country and to the world. He spoke out often and long about closure when he was in this House. He would abhor the approach the Government is using today in taking away the right of Parliament to investigate and speak about a Bill with which most of the people, we now believe, do not agree.
The Member for Calgary East (Mr. Kindy) made much of the fact that 75 per cent of the Members in this House want this Bill. That is a little bit of a sheepish approach to what happens in this House. Seventy-five per cent of the Members happen to be Conservatives. However, 75 per cent of the people did not vote for them. In fact, only approximately 50 per cent of the people across Canada voted to elect these 75 Members, so they cannot in any way say they represent more than 50 per cent of the population. In fact, their support has declined so much in the last little while, they would have a great deal of trouble suggesting that they now represent more than 30 per cent or 35 per cent of the population. Perhaps a third of the people in the country would agree with the Government, but we do not think that even that many would agree with the Government on this particular piece of legislation. When 40 advocacy groups felt they had some need to speak to this Bill and came before the rushed hearings, not one of them expressed support for this particular piece of legislation. Forty groups came before the parliamentary committee and not one expressed support for this particular piece of legislation.
1 spoke about my predecessor from Prince Albert. He spoke loud and long against closure in this House. He believed that this kind of approach to legislation, this kind of closing off of Parliament, was anti-democratic. He would be aghast if he saw what was happening today. Many people who are watching this debate today will remember the pipeline debate on which Mr. Diefenbaker spoke quite often. He took the idea of closure to the people of Canada and they rejected that as a method of getting legislation through Parliament.
The Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker was not the only Conservative who thought that closure was not a good idea and who spoke against it. Not too long ago, on June 9, 1981, one of the members of this particular Government, the Party that controls this House right at the moment, one of the frontbenchers, made a few statements about closure. It was the Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), the Minister for International Trade. He stated:

This comes from a closure-crazed government-

-a government which suffers from the crime of parliamentary bestiality. It
cannot wait to force these kinds of things through the House.
He went on to say that it is a betrayal of the parliamentary system. We have a parallel here today.
