To go on with the comments of the Member for St. John's West on the subject of closure, he said:
This is an illustration of what has happened to Canada. Today we have a parliamentary system of government without any checks and balances and without the separation of powers. The Prime Minister has a group of docile sheep in his caucus who keep him in power, no matter what he is doing. They just say, "Baaa, sir, baaa, sir, pass it through the House, sir". As long as they do that, he has absolute power.
That sounds very much as though he were speaking about his own Government, doesn't it, Mr. Speaker? He continued:
This Prime Minister has absolute power as long as the majority in his caucus give him that unlimited power. They are so busy with their noses in the patronage trough and power trough that they neither know nor care what happens to this Parliament, and we can expect nothing from them.
That is what the Member from St. John's West, the present Minister for International Trade, thought of closure when he sat on the opposition side of the House.
I will go on with further comments by that particular Minister. He said:
Where are all the defenders of the people on the other side of the House? They are going to come out of their trough in a few minutes. They will hear the bell and they will have to break away from whatever trough they have their noses in at the moment. They will have to come into this House and say "Oink, oink". They will have to say "Aye, aye". They will have to say "Yes" to the stampeding of Parliament, to rushing this bill through the House. They will have to say "Yes" to the gutting of Parliament. They will have to do the dirty work that the parliamentary assistants, assassins and eunuchs have asked them to do.
I think that most of the Members of this House would agree that what is being done here is not good parliamentary procedure. This particular Bill is probably a good example of the inadequacy that the Government has shown during its four years in this House. It promised that it would do something about child care four years ago in the election campaign. It has been in office for four years now and it did not move on this issue until just lately. The Bill was introduced for second reading in the middle of the summer when the election call was imminent. Parliament was asked to give it second reading in the middle of the summer, and the Government is now moving closure on a Bill that had only one speaker from each Party at third reading.

September 22, 1988
Time Allocation
Why is there such a rush to push this legislation through this Parliament if it is so unpopular? Could it be that the Government does not want the people of Canada to hear too much about this legislation because it happens to be a centre-piece of its election program, that it wants to put it before the people of Canada as a plank in its election program? If the people hear too much about how poor this legislation is, they will not support the Government in this particular area.
I abhor, as did the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, a Government that will push through Parliament, without adequate debate, any legislation which should have a full airing before the people of Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-144
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to speak to the time allocation motion that has been brought forward by the Government to limit debate and to effect closure. This abuse of the democratic process by a majoritari-an Government is the worst in the history of Canada. Most people who watch Parliament or are interested in Parliament are really not aware of the procedures of the House. I would like to say a few words based on that lack of awareness of some, or perhaps of the majority.
I believe that we have abused the democratic process through the Government's operation in more than one instance. In fact, most Bills that have been of prime importance have ended up with time allocation. Why, with such a massive majority, has the Government not been able to manage its own business? When it cannot manage its own business it tries to scapegoat. It tries to scapegoat the Senate. The amusing yet sad story is that the Senate has not yet even seen this Bill and yet the Government is saying that it is blocking it. That is perfectly ridiculous.
What has been the procedure on this very important piece of legislation, this basic building block to equality, stature, and opportunity for all Canadians? Let us look at what has taken place in order to know where we stand. Twenty years ago a Royal commission under Florence Bird, now Senator Bird, took a good look at what was happening with equality of opportunity for women and families in this land. She noted that one of the important measures to effect equality for women and for families was the application and implementation of child care.
The Canada Assistance Plan then came in which allowed for the growth and development of a child care policy for those who wished to apply for it. We had an evaluation done by Judge Abella. She was looking at equality of opportunity in the workplace and she developed the term "employment equity". That term related to the basic building block which was child care.
Then we had the report *1 Equality For All which looked at the application of Section 15 of the Canadian Constitution. We addressed the question of child care in that. We then had a parliamentary committee study child care. I sat on that
parliamentary committee. I went to British Columbia and heard what they had to say out there.
There was a lot of consultation. The Government is very good in consultation. The one thing it forgets is to listen to what is being said in the consultations. It came back and wrote a Bill. That means it supposedly put into legislative language the attitudes and concerns that were expressed.
After having this full and comprehensive review we were faced with the draft language of the child care legislation, Bill C-144. It has been available for review and study for some time and the Government now feels the pressure to convene this kangaroo court and call closure.
Let us take a look at the facts. The facts are that first reading was given on July 25, and today is September 22. It has not even been before the public to be looked at for two months. On July 25 the legal language came out. No one saw it on July 25, in the middle of what happened to be a very hot summer. On August 11 the Bill received second reading. There were not even three full days of debate. Eleven back-bench Conservatives spoke, six Members from our Party and six New Democratic Party Members spoke to the Bill. It was then sent to committee. The action taken by that committee was absolutely unprecedented. I know that many names were submitted, but of the list that was submitted, 40 witnesses appeared, each with half an hour in which to give an assessment of a Bill that was barely a month old.
Most of these groups are volunteers. They had to organize their members, sit down and work hard to analyse the Bill. It is not easy to get organized in the summer, but they came here and were treated with absolute disdain. These groups were given 30 minutes each to make a presentation and answer questions. How can one have an enlightened approach with that kind of ridiculous structure?
Not one group agreed with this Bill. All of them thought that it did not represent the years of consultation that had taken place. How can the Government say that it was listening? How can it be proud of this Bill? No wonder that it has called for closure. It does not want to arouse public interest and make Canadians aware of the disgraceful way the Government has handled the principles of democracy and justice, let alone being informed about the most important social policy that it is supposed to be introducing. It will not even bring in national objectives. This Bill is a sheer and utter disgrace and the Government ought to be ashamed of itself.
The Government operates by sleight of hand. It packages its policies with pretty words, says much in its preambles, but when it comes to putting it into legislation where it can actually put its words into practice, it has done nothing that will be effective for the children of this country.
September 22, 1988

What the Government is doing to the children is disgraceful. It will be called to account. It should reconsider the fact that it is calling closure on a vital piece of legislation which should ensure the future of Canadian children through choice by parents in Canada. That is not what the Government has done. This Bill will impact on our children and their families. The Government has put the country into a strait-jacket and it should be ashamed.
How can the Government expect the population to be informed when it ensures that it will be uninformed? How does it expect the Senate to respond when it has not yet sent the Bill there?
We should consider why the Government has developed this jackboot mentality. It does not bring forward the kinds of Bills this country deserves and has demanded. Democracy has lost its meaning. Time allocation and closure are totally unacceptable.
The 40 witnesses who had one-half hour each to comment on the Bill at least had time to say that it is flawed. That committee stage terminated on August 24. Report stage commenced on September 15. There were 13 amendments, only one of which was accepted.
I may have had complaints about the Broadcasting Act, but at least the Minister had been open enough to act in a spirit to accept some amendments. The Chairman of our legislative committee was sensible and open enough to allow an extension of time in order to hear the groups. It is unfortunate that this was not reflected in the Bill and in the amendments, but there was at least a sense of democracy. There is no sense of democracy or understanding with this legislation.
Finally, at third reading three Members have spoken on this vital and key social policy. It just shows what the Government thinks about social policy. It does not know how to implement social policy so it will hide it by passing it quickly so no one knows what it involves. The Government's approach is sheer hypocrisy.
It may be sheer hypocrisy and the Government may believe that it can cover it up, but the election will give us a chance to tell the people of Canada that while the Conservatives may know how to package policies through public relations, they know nothing about content.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-144
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to this motion of time allocation, which is really a form of closure. It is a disgrace that this Parliament is being presented with a motion like this today.
Government Members suggest we do not want to get this legislation through because we do not care about children. I hesitate to say that there are members of the Government who have not read the legislation because if they care about children they would recognize that this legislation does not focus on children.
Members opposite say that this is progressive legislation, but they cannot stand to hear debate about it. They are concerned
Time Allocation
about an open debate on this legislation. They restricted the number of witnesses at committee stage over a period of two days. Some 40 groups presented briefs and made representations to the committee, and the Government could not find one group in this country that supported the legislation.
These groups have done much research and study into child care, child development, public policy and family policy. Yet the Government could not find one group to support its legislation. The Government brought this legislation back from committee and allowed three Members to speak on what the Government suggests is historic social policy. There is no historic policy in front of the House. It is a cosmetic package that pretends to present a child care strategy. The Government is essentially allowing tax exemptions for people who already have child care. The Government is not looking after those two million children across Canada who are in dire need of child care.
I take exception to the suggestions by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and other members of the Government that as soon as this legislation is passed working mothers who are concerned about adequate care for their children will have that care available. That is utter nonsense and really misleads the public.
Not only did the Government restrict the number of people it would hear, it heard no one from Saskatchewan, the Maritimes or the Territories. Obviously, in its arrogant stance, the Government decided that these people were not important and that families and children in these areas did not count. I am sure the Government must have beaten the bushes to find someone who would support this legislation but was unable to do so. It could not find any group that would say this is good legislation.
In the 1984 election campaign the Conservatives said that there was need for child care policy. In a public debate the Prime Minister said that it would be a priority of his Government.
Let us look at how the Prime Minister considers this a priority of this Government. He waited until the summer of 1988 to bring forward legislation that he said was a priority. In the meantime, he was busy attempting to deindex seniors' pensions, he was deindexing family allowance, he was increasing the taxes on ordinary families and he was bailing out banks. He did absolutely nothing with respect to child care.
Then he rushed this legislation through in the summer of 1988, during the month of July when many people are on vacation and it is difficult to organize communities to have the kind of participation that something as important as this should have. Even at that it is not enough to cut off the ordinary people across the country. But what the Government is doing is refusing to allow a full and open debate on the child care legislation that has been brought before us.

September 22, 1988
Time Allocation
To suggest that it is putting all this extra money into child care is absolute nonsense. We know that in the next seven years we certainly would, under the Canada Assistance Plan, get the same number of spaces as we would have now. We also know that what would happen is that we would not cut off the Canada Assistance Plan, which is going to happen now, as soon as the provinces decide that they want to become part of this plan. It means that many of those families that are in real need, the families of low-income and poor families, are the ones that are not going to be able to get access to child care. That is a real disgrace.
We have seen the effects of what happened under an insensitive Government in wartime. Certainly we are redressing today some of the things that happened to Japanese Canadians. If this measure goes through, what it is really saying again is that we have an insensitive Government that does not care about what happens to our children in the present or our children in the future.
This kind of child care strategy is no child care strategy at all. What the Government is doing is deleting the ability to use the Canada Assistance Plan. What it is doing is allowing for tax expenditures to be part of the expenditure of the child care program, which really is not adding to spaces at all. What it is doing is putting money into the pockets of the people who now can afford child care. That is not the issue at all. The issue is the two million children out there who have no kind of quality care.
There has been some talk about how maybe we as the New Democratic Party would like to centralize all of the delivery of that service. We are certainly not talking about that at all. This Party would like to see a decentralization of service with some guarantee that there would be quality care, whether one is in the Northwest Territories, Yukon, Newfoundland, British Columbia, Quebec, Ontario, or wherever. That certainly is not central control. What it is saying is that any child in Canada has the right to some quality care. This Government has consistently refused to put in any kind of national objectives. Sometimes 1 wonder how members of this Government think they grew up themselves. It seems to me that they love to talk about it being fine if parents would stay at home and look after their children.
I think we have to look at the reality that if we take the lowest salary of the two-income family away we will find that 64 per cent of those families are living in poverty. Two people are not working just for the luxury of working. Two people in a family today are working because they are trying to provide a home, a shelter, education and nurturing for their children.
Surely the Government should recognize that its responsibility is to be able to assist that. It does not matter where Canadians and Canadian families are living. It is most important that we have some kind of a child care policy that says that those children are guaranteed quality care. But this Government is insensitive. It is uncaring. It likes to package things in a cosmetic, superficial way that pretends it is doing things when it is doing nothing. It is terrified to expose itself to
an open debate in which the Canadian people can really understand what a sham this legislation is. This is an insult to the intelligence of Canadians.
The only good thing that can happen is that we have an election soon so that the Canadian people can make a judgment on the kind of legislation we will have before us. This Government will not allow it to happen in the House of Commons because it will not allow that kind of debate. All it does every time it brings something in is to hurry it through and then decide right away that we must have closure we must have time allocation. That is because the Government cannot allow the people to debate this because they might understand what it is all about.
I see that my time is up. I hope that the time of this Government is up fairly soon.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-144
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you said, and rightly so, this is not really a debate on the substance of the Bill before the House, Bill C-144. I am sure Canadians would like to know what this Bill is about. And in fact it is an Act to authorize payments by Canada toward the provision of child care services and to amend the Canada Assistance Plan in consequence thereof.
The debate we are having right now is not, however, about the substance of the Bill but about procedure. This is one more instance, and I see my Quebec colleagues are very interested in the debate, this is one more instance of the Government bringing in a very important Bill and deciding to push it through the House and impose it on Canadians.
This is a very important Bill. This is a Bill that was promised us in 1984, during that great and glorious election campaign. And then all of a sudden, on July 25, 1988, four years later... Is the House to blame? Certainly not! Is the Opposition to blame? Not at all! It's all because one day the Government decided to get out its 1984 election platform and realized, in the process, that. . . Oh, dearie me! In 1984 we promised them a day care Bill, and we haven't done anything about it. Let's set a bill drafted, good or bad, and use our majority to push it through the House. We have to make sure that in the next election campaign, we can go to Quebec and everywhere else in Canada and say that we fulfilled our election mandate. Well, this is against all the rules of intelligent procedure in this House.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, we have tried to update the House of Commons and the way we operate. We had this vast parliamentary reform that was supposed to give parliamentary committees enough time to consider a bill and allow them to call witnesses to ensure that Canadians and Quebecers understand what the Bill entails. However, the Government is getting nervous because it realizes that the end is near, and so its says: whether you like it or not, we are going to push this Bill through, whether it is a good Bill or not. As far as I am concerned, it can't be that good, since only four witnesses were heard in three or four days, and none spoke out in favour of the Bill, so why the rush to limit debate?
September 22, 1988

Well, it seems there may be an election pretty soon. It doesn't matter whether the Bill is good or bad. The Government must be able to go before Canadians and say it has fulfilled its mandate. Quebecers, however, should wonder why the Government waited so long. Why did it wait until the very last minute-we want to introduce this Bill we just happened to overlook! I really have the impression that someone must have looked at their election platform and their promises, then reached the conclusion that a number of important items had been forgotten and, in the end-of-session panic decided to get those last promises through the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, this is not a healthy way to operate in a parliamentary democracy. The Government had four years and a month to schedule the implementation of its election promises.
This Government had four years, four long years, to implement this piece of legislation. Here we are, almost at the very last minute of the last two weeks-maybe, as my colleague from the third Party is saying-when the Government seems to have reopened the book of its promises of 1984 and realized that it has forgotten a few items in it, not to say many, and therefore will force, ram through the House of Commons, this issue.
I can imagine a Cabinet session where the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his Cabinet instruct Mr. Lewis, the Deputy House Leader, by saying "I don't care how you do it, ram this through the House because we may call the election". Who knows? Maybe Mr. Bourassa will call a provincial election. If such were the case, then there would be no federal election. That is what I heard this morning, and I will not give too much credit to that. But anything can happen.
Why is there this sudden urgency? It is a bad Bill. How can everybody who is involved in this subject matter be opposed to it? I am not an expert in this domain, but 1 hope I have enough intelligence to understand that everybody who is involved in this subject matter should oppose the Bill.
I know that in my district, especially the new one, I will most likely have the honour to run in the next election. I was already chosen there on May 1 with over a thousand people in attendance without being opposed, on a Sunday afternoon, with all my provincial Liberal friends present-two Ministers plus a few others, plus the municipal councillor. It just shows that sometimes in Montreal we can work together. In that district, this subject matter is extremely important and I am very sensitive to this subject matter.
My father was a doctor, and he delivered over 9,000 babies. Many of them are now having babies in my district. But since my father's days, society has changed dramatically. Society has changed unbelievably. Some people cannot adjust to these changes.
Time Allocation
We may like to revert back to the good old days of yesterday, but we cannot. I see these single parents having to cope with working, being on welfare, and having and raising children. It is extremely difficult. It is extremely difficult in the kind of area where I live. They cannot cope with that. They are discouraged. They do not understand why a rich society like Canada cannot have a tough first-class day care system for our future citizens.
I keep saying that this is the best investment that we can make. If we want to have a prosperous Canada, a good Canada, a new Canada, we must have a very strong population. Youth must be capable of replacing us. But they will have to face a greater difficulty than we have known, than my friend from Alberta has known, than we have all known in our youth. It was easier for us in our youth. But not today.
We must help these people who are most in need of help. We must provide for them the quality and the care that is expected in a civilized country like Canada.
I regret to say that we do not see this help in this project. It is long forgotten. It was put forward to the Canadian people in 1984 and it was suddenly reinvented on the very eve of an election. 1 do not like the urgency of ramming it through the House as it is being done now, after very little debate and after no consultation. After having rejected every plea of every expert in the domain, the Government intends to go ahead anyway. I do not think that that is good, and it does not reflect the spirit of the reform that we have had in the House of Commons.
Therefore, I will definitely vote against the fact that this Bill is being imposed so rapidly on the House of Commons, without having any real and honest debate and any real consultation, and without flexibility from the Government to listen to those who oppose it. A lot of these experts should not be taken for fools. They know what they are talking about, and they oppose the Bill. If they all collectively opposed the Bill, I do not see how I could give my consent to that Bill.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-144
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, want to join in this debate on time allocation.
The Conservative Government, 1 think, will go down in history as a four-year Government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-144
speechtext: Wishful thinking.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-144
speechtext:
It is a Government which was only elected for four years, but a Government which wasted a lot of time throughout those four years by not dealing with commitments that it made to the people of Canada while deciding at the last minute to rush a number of things through. Child care legislation is one such example. We did not get it until the summer, in a session that was not supposed to happen in the first place. Once again, because of government mismanagement of the business of the Commons, it was unable to bring forward any kind of concrete action until the eleventh hour. That action that it brought forward is flawed.

September 22, 1988
Time Allocation
I hope to have an opportunity, whenever the Government brings the Bill forward for debate, to speak to the issues within the child care Bill, the areas that point out why we disagree with what the Government is doing.
Let me deal for a few moments with the process that is basically taking away the right of this Parliament, of this Chamber, to debate substantive matters. It is not forever and ever, but for a reasonable period of time, so that members of the opposition Parties and members of the government Party can state their respective cases. In some cases, yes, we repeat particular aspects of those concerns. But we are a diverse lot here. We represent this country. We come from different areas. We have different needs, whether it is in child care or municipal infrastructure or redress to our citizens who have been abused in the past.
That is what the Commons is all about. It is a meeting place of representatives of the people from one end of this country to the other, from the American border to the Arctic Circle and beyond, to come together to speak on behalf of all Canadians.
If the Government is going to move immediately to restrict debate at third reading, or at report stage, or at second reading, then it is limiting our ability and our right, in fact, to represent our constituents properly.
Since I have been in this House, 1 have seen time and time again not only how the Government has abused its powers, but how totally it made a mockery of majority government.
Time and time again I have seen the Government move closure at a time when anybody who is the least bit familiar with the rules of this House would know that within two, three or four more hours of debate it would have collapsed.
We have within our Standing Orders provision that for the first eight hours, 1 believe it is, after the first round of speeches, speeches are 20 minutes in length, followed by 10-minute question and answer periods, and after that eight hours of debate we are into 10-minutes speeches. One does not need to be a mathematician or have a computer to do a count of the bodies on this side of the House. Regretfully, there are many fewer of us than there are of government Members. Even moving motions that would refer the matter back to committee for six months or send it into nowhere for six months do not add much more time to the debate.
The reality is that the Government will get its legislation, no matter how we may feel about it and no matter what attempts we may make to delay it. I want to remind my hon. colleagues that my Party and the Liberal Party co-operated at the start of this Government's mandate to bring in reforms that eliminated some of the tools that were available to opposition Parties. Quite frankly, these were tools that the Conservatives used when in opposition to tie up Parliament, not for a few hours,
not for a day or two, but for weeks. We accepted those changes because we recognized that in a democratic society and in a parliamentary system, the Government of the day does have the constitutional right to legislate. Our job as opposition Members is to review, to challenge, to test and, yes, to oppose. By opposing, we hope we can push the Government of the day to make changes to legislation.
We have been successful at making changes. There is not one Bill with which I have dealt as a critic for my Party in which I have not been able to achieve some changes. Sometimes the changes make a good Bill a bit better, sometimes they make a bad Bill a bit better, but they are changes nonetheless. Those changes were not made just because 1 sent the Government a letter saying that I wanted these changes. I had to plant seeds, encourage and fertilize the ideas, so that the Government recognizes why those changes are important to make or why particular measures have to be thrown out, much as we did with the cost recovery clause in the Canada Shipping Act. It took a long time. It took a lot of networking in the marine industry to put pressure on the Government. It took time in the House, but that time gained us much. It gained us a better Bill without a clause that would cripple a particular industry.
I have seen the Government make many mistakes. What the Government does not realize it is doing by introducing time allocation on Bill C-I44, the child care Bill, is waving a red flag, not in the House but in the other place. It is giving legitimacy to that ancient body down the way, giving it the excuse to delay because the House of Commons legislative committee was not allowed to travel across Canada to hear witnesses. It was forced to stack 40 witnesses into a two-day period, witnesses every one of which was opposed to the current legislation.
The Government is playing into the Senate's hands by distorting the way in which this House operates, by making a mockery of the legislative process which is designed to ensure that the public of Canada, the citizens who quite frankly pay our bills and to whom we are responsible, has a chance to understand legislation and its ramifications. We believe strongly that what the Government is doing in the child care Bill is wrong. It is the wrong direction. We are prepared to fight that here in the House and on the hustings.
I say as well that it is important that we allow the House to work properly, to ensure that there is reasonable debate. We should avoid the attitude that we have to get it out of here and into the Senate because there may be an election call and we have to get it through. The reality is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will call the election when his pollster tells him he has a chance of getting a majority Government.
September 22, 1988

We could be playing this game of chicken, rushing things through the House, from now until next spring. Yet every week the Government will say that we have to rush things through. If the Government were that serious about child care, why was this Bill not placed on the Order Paper in the fall of 1984? Where was the urgency then? Where was the urgency for a lot of the other things we are seeing happening at the last minute like building roads and pipelines? One would think a municipal election was coming up the way the Government is doling out money to try to bolster its support.
1 realize that my time is almost up. 1 regret that once again the Government has decided to use its majority to push through this legislation. Representatives of the people of Canada, members of the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party, have listened to the key people involved in child care, the ones who are responsible for trying to provide the spaces and the services. Every one of them said that this Bill should go. 1 regret that the Government, instead of listening to them and to the Opposition, has decided to ram the Bill through this House, waving the red flag in front of the Senators. 1 can guarantee that it is all for naught.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-144
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too should like to join in this debate and denounce the Government which, for one reason or another, is always prepared to impose closure and cut short our parliamentary debates.
For openers, Mr. Speaker, let me make it clear at the outset that it was this Government which in the early days of its mandate raised the issue of parliamentary reform. We in the Opposition co-operated with the Government precisely because we believe that indeed Parliament is the appropriate forum to debate legislation such as this measure on child care. So this is a major issue in our society and there should be no need to resort to the kind of tactics this Government used in the past when it was on this side of the House. We all vividly remember that when the Conservative Party was in Opposition it kept the bells ringing for two weeks.
Now that we are dealing with an important piece of legislation like child care, the Government could hardly wait for the official Liberal opposition critic and the NDP Member to finish their speeches before bringing in closure. Mr. Speaker, is that what the Conservative Government had in mind when it began selling parliamentary reform to Members of all Parties in this House? What a scandalous contrast. When the Conservatives were in Opposition they tried every trick in the book to upset the parliamentary timetable of the then Government, but now that they sit on the Treasury benches they lower the boom and will not let the democratically elected Members have their say.
Mr. Speaker, 40 witnesses appeared before the parliamentary committee which considered this Bill. The 40 witnesses were allowed a measly half hour each. They were paraded before the committee one after another like sheep. This way in,
Time Allocation
and this way out. Thirty minutes each! All 40 of them denounced the Bill. So, Mr. Speaker, the fact that not a single organization came before the parliamentary committee to give its views on the legislation and that all 40 witnesses did speak out against it would indicate that something is wrong with the Bill. And we are supposed to be here to debate and correct defective legislation.
If the Government sets a limit on the time allocated pursuant to the Standing Orders and under the parliamentary reform proposed and adopted by this Government with the cooperation of the opposition Parties, we cannot speak out, we cannot even attempt to improve this Bill which everybody has found seriously lacking. How can we be expected to rise in this debate and support this measure?
Mr. Speaker, I used the word demagogy. The Government would have us believe that Canadians need this Bill if we are to upgrade the child care system, but we know full well that the Bill as drafted will not produce anything worthwhile. First they say it will be phased in over seven years, Mr. Speaker, so what do we do about the urgent needs of the people?
Mr. Speaker, the truth is that we are headed straight for the hustings! Belatedly, after wasting time for four years, the Government-
After mismanaging the time of the House for four years, now all of a sudden the Government gets a social conscience and says: "We need some social legislation. What about child care?" This was a promise which the Tory Party made in 1984. Here, on the eve of the election, they say: "Why not? Let's rush to the House. Let us put the gas on this piece of legislation and muzzle all the democratic rules," which the same Government introduced and approved. That is how disgusting this attitude is at the end of a Government's term of office. I am sure Canadians will remember that. We are going to make sure Canadians remember that.
The legislation is not even in the Senate yet, but the Government is blaming it for blocking the Bill. How can the Senate block it when the legislation is still here in the House of Commons? That is how the Tories' minds work at this time because they are planning an election and they are doing everything they can so that they can again con Canadians and make believe, as they did in 1984, that they can do beautiful things. But once they get into office and get power they do the opposite. That is what we are talking about here today.

Mr. Speaker, I simply must speak out against this unacceptable and shameful Government approach. We will do everything we can to reject undemocratic practices which fly in the face of the parliamentary reform we began in the fall of 1984 shortly after we were all elected to come here to Ottawa.

September 22, 1988
Time Allocation
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, I think this measure is unacceptable, but if the government Members really thought it was good, why did they not introduce it sooner? If the Government is convinced that it is a good Bill and that Canadians will accept it, call an election right now and give them a chance to say what they think of the Bill. If the Government is re-elected the Bill will pass right then and there. However I am sure that the people will not accept the Bill, and so we will do everything we can to bury it, Mr. Speaker.
Mr. Speaker, just so our listeners will understand exactly what we are saying and why this Government chose to take such an antidemocratic and totalitarian approach-debate has been cut off-certain dates will make it clear for the listeners why this debate is so important and why we are opposed to this antidemocratic measure.
Mr. Speaker, let us just say that four years ago we were given a list of committees, reports, studies, commissions and what have you, much too long to go into details here. I might simply refer to a few recent dates. On July 13, 1988, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) who is sponsoring this Bill announced that something like $1 billion would be made available and that 200,000 additional spaces would be created. We wonder what that is going to solve over a seven-year period. Given the extent of the problem, Mr. Speaker, that is just like a drop in the bucket.
But the Bill was first introduced on July 25, 1988, so there was a waste of time right there. Had the Government been really serious and intent on having Parliament adopt this legislation before the elections it would have tabled the Bill on July 13, minutes after the Minister's statement. No, it chose to wait until July 25, twelve days later. And now they want us to pass it in one day, after 40 witnesses appeared to say it is not good enough. They expect the Senate to do the same thing in 24 hours. Well now, Mr. Speaker! Is that democracy, or are we up against Conservative dictatorship? I am sure that Canadians will not stand still for this kind of procedure.
Mr. Speaker, you are signalling that my time has expired. I thank you for your attention and consideration, and again I want to say that this approach is not in keeping with the spirit of the parliamentary reform which this Government has implemented with the full support of both opposition Parties, the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party. Within the bounds of democracy, Mr. Speaker, we will do everything we can to prevent this Government from generating into a dictatorship here in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER THIRD READING STAGE OF BILL C-144
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words during this time allocation motion moved by the Government yesterday. 1 oppose the allocation of time on the Bill before the House today, a Bill on child care, and I do so for a number of reasons.
First I want to remind you, Mr. Speaker, because you were not a Member of Parliament before 1984, that prior to 1984 the Conservative Party used to complain loudly and clearly about the Liberal Government in those days invoking time allocation over and over again. I suspect that if you were to go
back through the records you would find that the Conservative Government is invoking time allocation at least as often as the Trudeau Government did, perhaps even more often than the Trudeau Government did in its many years of office.
I know the two senior Alberta Members across the way, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) and the Hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) are probably very discouraged that their Party is cutting off debate, using time allocation, bringing down the parliamentary guillotine in the same way that the Trudeau Government did year in and year out. In fact, I know the Member from Bow River would like to get up in the House now and criticize the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) for cutting off debate, freedom of speech, and invoking time allocation after only one speaker from each political Party. I cannot recall in my 20 years in Parliament a Government before that brought in time allocation or closure after only one speaker from each of the political Parties. I know the Member from Bow River, who served many years as a Social Credit Member in the Province of Alberta, who was also a Cabinet Minister, and who defeated the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) for a nomination to run for the federal House of Commons, has never seen this happen before.
I would be interested to hear him speak his mind. I know after a long and distinguished career he is going to retire from this place. Perhaps he could go out with a burst of glory by speaking out, defending democracy in this country and freedom of speech. I know it must bother him, he is a man who generally speaks his mind.
I appeal to you, Mr. Speaker, and to Members across the way not to be afraid of the Prime Minister, to speak their minds, and to say: "We need more than one day of debate on third reading on child care and that after one speaker per Party it is neither right nor fair nor democratic to have time allocation or closure brought in at the end of this debate".
At one time this would be absolutely unheard of. In fact, the Conservative Party across the way used to complain when the Liberals brought in closure after four, five, seven, or eight days of debate. I remember sanctimonious speeches on this side of the House. The Tories would ring the bells, storm the Chair, and do all kinds of things in protest against an undemocratic Government across the way. How people change once they get into office. How the leopard changes his spots once he is in office. If you were not in the chair, I am sure you would like to get up and complain about the cutting off of debate. I know that is exactly what is on your mind as a fair-minded lawyer from Montreal. I am sure you have looked back in the old debates to see John Diefenbaker, Jed Baldwin, and all the Conservative Party Members complaining about Liberal after Liberal cutting off debate. Where is parliamentary supremacy? Here 1 see the young man, the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling), who I understand is running as a Member again. I commend him for that.
September 22, 1988

1 imagine he too must be disturbed that his Prime Minister invoked closure after only one speaker per Party on child care. It has never happened before in the history of this Parliament. I am sure, unless he wants to be a cabinet Minister after the next election, that he will rise and speak his mind. Ele must be disturbed about what is going on.
I see that I am being so persuasive you are cutting me off, so I will sit down and continue later.

subsubtopic: SITUATION OF CERTAIN FAMILIES LIVING IN CITY OF OTTAWA UNITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have in my constituency a number of families living in low-cost housing units owned by the City of Ottawa and managed by City Living, who are faced with excessive rent increases of up to 8.8 per cent for the current year. This is almost twice the then 4.6 per cent inflation rate. To make a bad situation worse, the poor state of repairs of some of those units forces tenants to board up their windows and even in some cases to condemn some rooms because the houses are too cold in winter.
Mr. Speaker, I feel this is an unfair and inhumane way to treat tenants who, because they do not earn high salaries and cannot afford a comfortable, well-insulated house, have to live in low-cost housing units. Those people are victimized.
In order to deal with the problem and help those people, I urge the Government to reinstate RRAP, the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, as to the municipalities eligibility to the program, so they can get federal support to rehabilitate, repair and perhaps better insulate their houses, in order that the tenants of those low-cost housing units in my constituency can live comfortably and be treated like full-fledged citizens for which we care.

Mr. Speaker, the Ukrainian community makes up a large part of Canada's
multicultural society. One of the best known members of that community, the late William Kurelek, is one of Canada's most accomplished artists.
Since 1983 we on Parliament Hill have been able to enjoy a significant work by the artist. The Canadian Pioneer, a six-panel mural, was acquired by the Government of Canada from the Niagara Falls Art Gallery. The mural depicts Kurelek's pictorial interpretation of the history of Ukrainian immigration to Canada. Since Canada's railway played such an important role in bringing Ukrainian pioneers to the West to settle, this work is appropriately displayed in the House of Commons Railway Committee Room.
The work's name and the artist's name are not identified at the present time. I think that this is unfortunate. I am sure that all Members would agree that such a noteworthy exhibit should be clearly identified for all to know and appreciate. Let us correct this oversight.

subtopic: CLAM DIGGING ON VANCOUVER AND GULF ISLANDS
CLAM DIGGING ON VANCOUVER AND GULF ISLANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since 1986 there has been a substantial increase in commercial clam digging on Vancouver Island and the Gulf Islands. Residents are under siege by diggers who harvest at low tides both day and night. There are few limitations on anyone seeking a commercial licence, and the number of diggers has increased dramatically as the price paid for clams has risen.
In response to my letter of November, 1987, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon), acknowledged complaints from Gulf Island residents. However, he did not offer any solutions at the time, and I am pursuing the issue with him once again.
A recent meeting of Salt Spring Island residents, organized by Island Trust, unanimously concluded that the whole island be closed to commercial clam harvesting. The meeting put forward recommendations calling for the creation of a federal-provincial investigation into commercial clam digging, new and tougher licensing regulations, harvesting limits, and designated commercial harvesting areas in accordance with local zoning regulations.
It is not enough to bring in size limitations and toughen up restrictions as to bag limits and the activities of these clam diggers, as the Minister of Fisheries has promised. Most important is the need to expand enforcement. The regional shellfish co-ordinator admits that there are not enough fisheries officers available to do the job.

September 22, 1988

Mr. Speaker, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) is challenging the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in order to cash in on his popularity and win the attention of Canadians. People in Canada certainly would be interested in knowing the motives and the arguments of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition on the following subjects: The quality of his leadership within the Liberal Party of Canada and his Party's financial position; his suggestions to the non-elected Liberal Senators who are holding Canadians hostages on matters of national import; his lack of understanding of the Free Trade Agreement, his insult to the Quebec Premier; the economic position Liberals left Canadians in when this Conservative Government came to power; the passive and active complicity of federal Liberals over these last 20 years in the area of the environment, because they are truly responsible for pollution in Canada.
When the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition is ready to answer those questions, let him say so, and Canadians will certainly be interested in hearing him apologize and contradict himself.

maintopic: BROILER HATCHING EGGS-CALL FOR IMPORT CONTROLS
BROILER HATCHING EGGS-CALL FOR IMPORT CONTROLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian broiler hatching egg industry needs border controls on hatching eggs and chicks.
In November, 1986, the Canadian Broiler Hatching Egg Marketing Agency was established, having as signatories the Provinces of Alberta, Manitoba, Ontario, and Quebec, thus representing 80 per cent of Canada's broiler hatching egg production.
The purpose of that exercise was to establish border controls on imports of these products under Article XI of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. Without such controls, the U.S. controls presently 60 per cent of breeder replacement pullet growers, 90 per cent of the broiler hatching egg producers, and 14 broiler hatcheries are prevented from realizing fair returns to labour.
We need supply management in this industry. Before the last election the Conservative Government stated that it was in favour of supply management. Perhaps free trade has changed
its mind. If the Tories are still in favour of supply management, why do they not want to have this industry provided with the tools in order to have supply management for broiler hatching eggs?

subtopic: FULFILMENT OF COMMITMENT TO JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERNED DURING WORLD WAR II
FULFILMENT OF COMMITMENT TO JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERNED DURING WORLD WAR II
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in May, 1984, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), then the Leader of the Official Opposition, said: "Canadian citizens whose rights were abused and violated and trampled upon indeed should be compensated". He went on to say: "If there was a Conservative Government I can assure you we would be compensating Japanese Canadians".
Today that commitment has been kept. When history records the story of the Prime Minister and of this Government, and of this Parliament, the redress of Canadians of Japanese origin may very well be just a small footnote. Hopefully, however, that footnote will make it quite clear that this was their finest hour.

subtopic: TORONTO-PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENT'S FIRING OF JOHN SEWELL
TORONTO-PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENT'S FIRING OF JOHN SEWELL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, finally the Government has recognized that there is a housing crisis in Toronto. In Toronto itself there has been one individual more than anyone else who has tried to ensure that affordable housing is not a thing of the past. John Sewell has pushed strongly for more public housing. He has advocated the redesign of existing public housing units, and he has worked hard toward the goal of reducing profits in order to make housing more affordable.
Rather than being thankful for a job well done, the Ontario Housing Minister, and her boss, the Premier of the Province, gave Mr. Sewell his walking papers.
If the Ontario Minister of Housing and the Premier of that province were really serious about doing something to help the City of Toronto through the worst housing crisis in recent memory, they would not have fired the one person who, more than any other, was making a difference.
September 22, 1988

1 have some advice for the Government. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) wants Torontonians to believe that he is finally taking the housing problem seriously. That, it appears, is why the Downsview land was released last week. If the Government really wants to demonstrate that it means what it says, it should offer Mr. Sewell the job of overseeing the release of public lands in Toronto and co-ordinating a first-rate affordable housing program on the Downsview lands.
1 have discussed this with Paul and Mike Flaherty from the Toronto area who are present today, and that is what they think as well!

subtopic: TRANSPORTATION OF DANGEROUS GOODS THROUGH TORONTO
TRANSPORTATION OF DANGEROUS GOODS THROUGH TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Gilbert Task Force Report on the transportation of dangerous goods by rail through the Toronto area states that among the major causes of rail accidents are track operational and equipment deficiencies.
We recognize that railways provide economically and ecologically preferable modes of transport. Yet throughout this country for many, many years we have persisted in priorizing what we spend on air and highway transportation. If we were to spend on air and highway transportation a fraction of what we spend on improving railway equipment and track conditions, we would provide this country with safe and speedy transportation that would be much better in conserving the environment.
1 hope that among the points made in this task force report what will be taken with utmost seriousness will be the need to upgrade our equipment and track conditions.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is running around the country announcing billions of dollars of promises on a weekly basis in a desperate bid to shore up his Party's position in advance of an election campaign, I beg him to give pause for thought to old promises made and not kept. In July of 1984, the Prime Minister, in the heat of an election campaign, sent a telex to the Mayor of the City of Corner Brook, Newfoundland. In that telex he said: "I want to assure you of my and my Party's full support for the establishment of a federal forestry centre in Corner Brook, Newfoundland". He
said: "Statements to the contrary by the sitting Liberal M.P. are simply untrue". In July of 1988, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), Newfoundland's representative in the federal Cabinet, wrote a letter to the mayor in which he said: "There are simply no funds available. This decision is final and is not a contradiction of the Prime Minister's previous comments on the matter".
The people of western Newfoundland want to know two things; when is a promise not a promise? When is a contradiction not a contradiction? And how much is the paper the Prime Minister's commitment was written on worth because so far it has brought us nothing but a cynical view of the value of the Prime Minister's word and the commitments of this Government, in particular, the dog in the manger attitude of the Member for St. John's West who now wants to build that badly needed forestry centre in his own backyard? Newfoundland is bigger than just the City of St. John's.

subtopic: MINING EXPLORATION IN QUEBEC-ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT IN ABITIBI -TEMISCAMINGUE
MINING EXPLORATION IN QUEBEC-ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT IN ABITIBI -TEMISCAMINGUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Association des prospecteurs du Quebec had its 14th Annual Convention in Val d'Or from September 14 to 16. Over 620 members registered for the convention, the highest attendance ever recorded, a sign of the keen interest of Quebec prospectors in the mining industry.
Mr. Speaker, one of the conclusions of the convention was that 1988 was a difficult year for the prospecting sector in Quebec. This is partly due to the changes in mid-flight that were made in the flow-through shares system, at various levels of government, but especially to the stock market crash which had a severe impact on the mining industry.
During the convention, people from the prospecting sector sent a clear message to both levels of government, and I urge the Ministers of Finance to consider very carefully a number of demands that are aimed at giving a boost to an industry that is already flourishing and is very important to the development of Abitibi-Temiscamingue.
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to congratulate Mr. Guy Bourassa of Rouyn-Noranda, who was elected President of the Association des prospecteurs du Quebec for 1988-89. I am sure Mr. Bourassa will meet this challenge successfully, promoting the interests of the mining industry in our area.
I want to offer my full co-operation to the new President and to the Association des prospecteurs du Quebec.

September 22, 1988

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF VANCOUVER ISLAND NATURAL GAS PIPELINE PROJECT
ANNOUNCEMENT OF VANCOUVER ISLAND NATURAL GAS PIPELINE PROJECT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, British Columbians can be forgiven for being skeptical upon hearing news that the Conservatives have once again announced that they will build the long awaited, often promised Vancouver Island natural gas pipeline.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF VANCOUVER ISLAND NATURAL GAS PIPELINE PROJECT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF VANCOUVER ISLAND NATURAL GAS PIPELINE PROJECT
speechtext:
This was, after all, the same group of Conservatives-the ones applauding here-who promised the pipeline before the last federal election only to have the then Minister of Energy, the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney), and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) renege on their promise only weeks after the election. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to complete my remarks on time allocation. Before we broke for Question Period, I was saying that it was very strange to see the Conservative Party across the way bring in time allocation on the child care Bill after only one speaker from each Party has spoken in the House. I have not seen it happen before where time allocation was brought in so quickly by the government Party. I see across the way many long time Members of Parliament who were here in the days of the Trudeau Government when time and again they complained about time allocation and closure being brought in by that Government.
There are more occasions now when time allocation is brought in than there were in the previous five or 10 years. There are more occasions when time allocation is used than we had in the days when members of the Conservative Party complained. I see the Hon. Member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) hiding his head behind the newspaper in shame because of what his Government is doing.
I have here a copy of a speech made by the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) on June 9, 1981, when he complained about the Liberal Government bringing in time allocation. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) is very embarrassed and shouting from his seat.
1 wish to quote something stated by the Minister for International Trade when time allocation was brought in by a Liberal Government. He said:
The same little group comes in here on every closure motion. The same little group of parliamentary eunuchs, the same group of parliamentary assassins-the House Leader, the assistant House leader, the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans), the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres)-are in here all the time, assassinating this House and removing the good from the House. That is why 1 call them the parliamentary eunuchs. The good has already been removed from them.

September 22, 1988
Time Allocation
The Hon. Member was talking about parliamentary eunuchs in the Liberal Party. I do not disagree with him. However, now that the Conservative Party is in power it is doing exactly the same thing.
Back in 1981 the Minister for International Trade further stated:
Where are all the defenders of the people on the other side of the House? They are going to come out of their trough in a few minutes. They will hear the bell and will have to break away from whatever trough they have their noses in at the moment. They will have to come into this House and say "Oink, oink". They will have to say "Aye, aye". They will have to say "Yes" to the stampeding of Parliament, to rushing this bill through the House. They will have to say "Yes" to the gutting of Parliament. They will have to do the dirty work that the parliamentary assistants, assassins and eunuchs have asked them to do.
Now the Minister for International Trade is on the government side of the House. What is he doing? He is bringing in time allocation, closure, and asking his mindless backbenchers, who are now the new parliamentary eunuchs, to get up and approve what he wants and approve what the Prime Minister wants in terms of cutting off debate on the child care legislation before the House.
I ask my friends across the way, and the Hon. Member for Burlington who is hanging his head in shame as he reads the newspaper, to get up on their hind legs and speak out in favour of parliamentary democracy. I say to my friend, the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling), who has been here for many years, that he must rise and say the same thing now that he is in government as he said when he was in opposition, that Parliament should not be throttled, that parliamentary debate must continue, and that the people of Canada must have their say.
For years I remember John Diefenbaker sitting in the corner of the House to the left of the Speaker and rising and saying time and again that the Governments of the day were not allowing a full and complete debate, and saying that there had to be full parliamentary participation.
We have a Bill before the House today where there has only been one speaker per Party at third reading, and down comes the guillotine; a Bill before the House today where there were only two days of hearings in the City of Ottawa by the parliamentary committee that spent hundreds of thousands of dollars, and down came the guillotine; a Bill before the House today where the Province of Saskatchewan wanted to present a position and it was not heard.
The Province of New Brunswick was not heard, the Province of Nova Scotia was not heard, the Province of Prince Edward Island was not heard, nor was the Yukon or the Northwest Territories. Those provinces were not heard because the parliamentary committee only met for two days before the Government brought in closure.
Where is democracy? I ask some of the Members opposite, who used to be rugged individuals, who used to stand up and speak for freedom of speech and ask that the democratic
process play a role, to speak now. It would be interesting to see if the Minister for International Trade was correct when he spoke in 1981 about Liberal Government back-benchers being parliamentary eunuchs afraid to get up and say their piece. He said they were parliamentary sheep who would say "bah bah" in the House of Commons as they voted in favour of the Government bringing in time allocation.
Where is the Minister of Justice? He used to pretend to be so indignant when he was on this side of the House and the Liberals brought in time allocation. Where is he now? He is a yes-man for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). How can he agree now to impose time allocation when the Province of Saskatchewan did not have its chance to present its position on child care before the parliamentary committee? How can he do that as a senior Saskatchewan Minister? I am really shocked that the Minister of Justice who at one time was progressive, another John Diefenbaker defending parliamentary freedom, freedom of speech and the dignity of this institution, would now sit back with the power which has gone to his head and watch as his Prime Minister rides roughshod over the wishes of the people of Canada.
It is with a great deal of sadness that I speak today as I watch my friends opposite. For instance, our good old friend from Parry Sound-Muskoka, who has been here a long time, is hiding behind his newspaper. His head is sort of bowed in embarrassment. He is turning a bit redder all the time. Why does that Member not get up and speak now and ask the Government to withdraw this time allocation motion? How can he justify one speaker per Party? How can he justify only one day of debate on third reading of a very important Bill? There were over 40 witnesses at the committee and every single one was in opposition to this Bill.

I want the people of Canada to remember that here is a Party that likes to hold itself out as being the social conscience of Canada, but when we bring in the first child care program in the history of this country the NDP is out there blocking every move in order to thwart this program for the people of Canada. The New Democratic Party of Canada should be ashamed of itself. I think the next time the Member goes back to Saskatchewan-and we are all waiting for him to come back soon because we only see him there once in a while and it is a great pleasure for us-he will have some explaining to do. When he goes from Aylmer back to Saskatchewan I want him to tell the people of Saskatchewan why he, now the great defender of the Government of Saskatchewan, is blocking this legislation. Why is he standing shoulder to shoulder with the Senate of Canada, with Allan J. The House resumed from Tuesday, September 20, consideration of Bill C-136, an Act respecting broadcasting and to amend certain Acts in relation thereto and in relation to radiocommunication, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee; and the amendments of Mrs. Finestone:
Motion No. 71

"(3) The Minister shall consult with the Chairman before the Governor in
Council makes an appointment to the Board."
Motion No. 73
That Bill C-136 be amended in Clause 39 by striking out line 14 at page 26 and substituting the following therefor:
"hold office for a term not exceeding seven".
Motion No. 76
That Bill C-136 be amended in Clause 74 by striking out line 20 at page 45 and substituting the following therefor:

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first of these amendments relates to Clause 34. We were discussing the consultation between the Minister and the Chairman of the Board of CBC to ensure that there was no conflict of interest and that the members to be appointed by Governor in Council to that board were to be appointed in a way that would enrich the board to its fullest.
1 know that the Minister has made appointments to the board, and the last group of appointments she made were appointments of fine, qualified people of which all Canadians would be quite proud.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Including women.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Including women, right. It is true that those appointments have been good appointments. I would hope that the Minister to be appointed following the election that is about to take place will make the appropriate appointments as well based on those needs.
I would like to recommend the acceptance of this amendment because one has to prevent the perception of patronage appointments. I am sure the Minister would not want that perception to impinge on the making of proper appointments.
The second group of amendments in this grouping are Motions Nos. 73 and 76. They relate to the length of the term of service of both the President of CBC, as found in Clause 39, and the tenure of office of the officers and commissioners of the CRTC, as found in Clause 74. These motions, if passed, would provide that the appointment of the President of the CBC would be for a period of seven years and full-time appointments to the CRTC would be extended to a period of seven years.
These are key administrative and tribunal positions. It is important that the holders of these positions have the fullness of time in which to render the kind of decisions that will be in the best interests of the Canadian broadcasting system. I think it would further strengthen the arm's-length relationship between the corporation and the Government.
One of our concerns, from the very outset, has been of a tremendous potential for interference. Much of that has been removed, but I would strongly recommend that this measure be adopted to do the same thing.
Under Bill C-136, a Government would change the top management of two traditionally independent bodies during its term of office. The rule of a seven-year term for heads of Crown corporations is always intended to avoid this in order to protect the independence and to safeguard the arm's-length principle. At present, the President of the CBC, the Chairman of the CRTC, and the Governor of the Bank of Canada have been the significant exceptions to that rule. It was because of the very sensitive nature of the positions of the Governor of the Bank of Canada, the Chairman of the CRTC, and the President of the CBC that that was so.
Again, we do not want to have a sense of political interference with the increased patronage potential. Certainly, the perception of patronage appointments would exist because of the very nature of this change. Because of the structure of the CBC, with the chairman being a director of the board, it is most regrettable that we could not change that situation so we could determine who was the boss of the CBC, but it would have been a little too complex to make that amendment. Otherwise I would certainly have included in this amendment the position of the chairman of the board.
I would like to recommend that Motions Nos. 71, 73, and 76 be given very serious consideration and that they receive favour with the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald).

Recently we cross-examined Diane Lamb from Vancouver and Ron Collister, who, even though they are both Conservatives, are both pretty good people, and in spite of being Conservatives, they are good Conservatives. I was satisfied that while they had their own viewpoints on certain issues, these people were dedicated to protecting the interests of the CBC generally, and that was important.
That has not been true of all appointments made by the Government. Especially in the beginning of its term, not so much by this Minister but by her predecessors, appointments to cultural agencies including the CBC were dumping grounds for Tory patronage appointments for so-and-so's campaign manager, the Prime Minister's secretary, someone else's friend, and so on. They were pretty awful appointments, and the appointments recently got a lot better.
Motions Nos. 73 and 76 would extend the term of the President of the CBC and that of the CRTC commissioners to seven years. I think seven years is probably too long for one appointment. Indeed, I am told that the President of France- God knows how he loves his seven-year term-is considering a national referendum to shorten the presidential term to five years. If it is good enough for the President of France to shorten the term, we might consider that seven years might be a bit too long a term. As I said to Mr. Juneau in the committee hearings, it certainly avoids any messy by-elections or anything like that.
I would not support Motions Nos. 73 and 76 but would support Motion No. 71.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few comments in support of Motion No. 71 introduced by my colleague from Mount Royal. The clause she is seeking to amend provides that a person who is engaged in the production or distribution of program material suitable for use by a broadcasting undertaking may be appointed director of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation if that is not his or her main occupation.
1 should like to say a few words concerning the power of the Government to make appointments to boards of directors and to emphasize how important we think it is that individuals appointed to the boards of these corporations and agencies be quite familiar with their new environment and truly represent the interests of the various Canadian groups. I am referring of course to francophones who at times get hauled over the coals when it comes to appointments to such national bodies as the
Broadcasting Act
Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or the CRTC. I mention this because the Canadian Diaspora is divided into two majority groups. First we have the anglophone Canadians in general who see to it that their colleagues and fellow nationals are duly represented, and I agree with that.
Then there are the Quebecers who make sure they are represented on the various Government Boards, but then there are the minority groups. It has always been a problem for both anglophones in Quebec and francophones outside Quebec to be appointed to the CBC or the CRTC, for example. 1 was looking at the CRTC 1987-88 annual report and 1 am impressed, as was my colleague from Mount Royal, by the quality and especially the representation of women, and I am in favour of that. The point I want to make is that we have to be sure that the directors appointed by the Government-I hope the Minister will exercise that power in the future, maybe not this Minister but the Minister of Communications who will have to act with diligence and make sure that the appointees represent the Canadian community as a whole and that the various commissions, particularly the CRTC and the CBC, have people on the board who understand the aspirations of the official languages minority groups, that is anglophones in Quebec and francophones outside Quebec.
I should like to get back to what seems to be a problem these days, the famous TV5 network. I fail to understand why in the past two or three days, responsible and serious journalist Michel Vastel of the fairly respectable newspaper Le Devoir should always be referring to the problem which TV5 creates for French-speaking Canadians outside Quebec. Mr. Speaker, I can quote these articles in Le Devoir which constitute an attempt-not strong enough, 1 would suggest-to depict what I mean by fair representation of linguistic groups.
I see in today's Le Devoir a statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and 1 quote:
"TV5 is an excellent network and we will make it available everywhere"
Another nice promise! Hon. Members will recall that yesterday the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) and the chief executive of TV5 were also quoted in an article by Michel Vastel.
Mr. Speaker, I will quote word for word, what TV5's General Manager, James Baird, confirmed to Le Devoir, namely that "... Consortium de Television Quebec-Canada is getting ready to apply to the CRTC, within a week at the most, in order to offer TV5 to cable distributors in Englishspeaking Canada at a price lower than the 27 cents a month paid by Quebec subscribers ..." This is a serious promise indeed, and 1 think it is a step in the right direction. And to quote further: "It is felt within the Canadian Department of Communications that this application should be dealt with rapidly, as a regulatory matter by the CRTC, in order to allow early penetration by CTQC, the Consortium de television Quebec-Canada, of that market outside Quebec." Again it seems to me that this is a promise. They are saying: it is coming. I was told this week, I think it was Tuesday last, September 20, by the Minister herself, that I was impatient. Well, things have moved since then!

September 22, 1988
Broadcasting Act
Wednesday, September 21, and today, September 22, two good articles support my position, which is simply to widen the choice, the viewing grid, in order indeed to include the famous TV5, a Canadian government initiative that cost $1.6 million of Canadian money and that, in my view, is really needed to allow for the development of our official language minorities across Canada, giving them access not only to Radio-Canada's French services, but also to another network, TV5, which as we know is an international entreprise, to the extent it is a consortium of several countries-which Canada, France, Belgium, Switzerland and the province of Quebec-agreed to put that programming together.
I am sorry, but 1 have to quote from an article, again by Michel Vaste in today's Le Devoir:
Miss Flora MacDonald indicated to Le Devoir that regulatory arrangements
could be soon negotiated between TV5, the cable distributors and the CRTC.
The latter promised yesterday to deal "expeditiously" with any application.
But the Minister is here. I for one trust her. I think she is a Minister to be trusted. If she says to those newspapers people she is serious and really wants to help us, let her do so. As it seems to me, the least she could do is tell the CRTC's president, whom she herself appointed, to act, to do something positive. Let her tell Mr. Juneau: "Enough pussy- footing and dilly-dallying. Do something. The time has come to act on that, and we want TV5 to be accessible to English-language cable distributors outside Quebec so it can be relayed to French- language viewers outside Quebec!
It seems to me we are not asking that much, but it is all connected with this particular amendment. The kind of directors we have, the kind of people we have to make the decisions and recommendations all depends on how these people see their role. I see them as representatives of the diaspora. I also see them as strong representatives of various interest groups, including francophones, women, native people and multicultural groups. I think all these people should be very well represented. I think the Minister should give serious consideration to the amendment submitted by the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) which says the Minister should consult. That is all we want her to do. We want her to consult properly and at length before making appointments, so that we can be sure of the qualifications of the people up there, that they are really on top of the situation and can provide the kind of service that truly meets our expectations.
