Mr. Speaker, I want to make a very short intervention on the three motions before us. In terms of Motion No. 71, this would make it a requirement that the Minister would have to consult with the chairman of the CBC before any appointments were made. 1
see that as a protection for the Minister and for the board itself.
After an election and the enthusiasm of a new Government, whatever its stripe, rewards are made. Not immediately after the 1984 election but later, when there was a move to appoint new people to the board of Air Canada, we saw people being appointed not because of expertise in transportation or even expertise as a consumer of that particular mode of transportation. The best the person involved could come up with was that she had a driver's licence and a Tory card.
It makes sense to give the Minister the power to hold off the patronage boys. Whatever the structure is, whether it is a committee of the PMO or whatever, it ought to be able to say: "Hang on. Thank you for your suggestions. Let me take them back to the chairman of the CBC and take a look at the mix, the regional mix, and the level of knowledge and understanding of broadcasting, whether it is on the technical side or on the performing arts side".
Even though it may be done informally now, I suspect that there is that type of give and take. The Minister and the Government would not drop it on to the chairman and say: "Here is your new crew". There is some consultation. This is an added bit of protection so that the Minister cannot be overruled or forced to put some people on the board of the CBC who would not go with the wishes of the Minister herself or himself, whoever the Minister may be at the time.
1 encourage the Government to accept this amendment. It does not prevent it from making the appointments or unduly restrict it. It formalizes in law an informal process that occurs today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 75A states:
That Bill C-136 be amended in Clause 70 by striking out line 4 at page 44 and substituting the following therefor:
"7. Neither the Company, nor its parent, nor any".
Page 44, line 4, of the Bill states:
Neither the Company nor any person controlled by the Company shall directly or indirectly hold a licence issued under the Broadcasting Act or carry on a broadcasting undertaking within the meaning of that Act.

September 22, 1988
Broadcasting Act
That is contained in Part IV of the Act entitled "Amendments to Other Acts" and it refers to the Bell Canada Act. Clause 70 states:
Section 7 of the Bell Canada Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"7. Neither the Company nor any person controlled by the Company shall directly or indirectly hold a licence issued under the Broadcasting Act or carry on a broadcasting undertaking within the meaning of that Act".
The company, I gather, is Bell Canada. Both Motions Nos. 75A and 75B deal with Bell Canada. I read the amendment that we proposed. Bell, which is big enough to swallow up the whole broadcasting industry, cannot get involved with any undertaking under Bill C-136. That is what it states in the Act, unamended. However, Members could ask themselves if it involves all of Bell. Bell has this great ability, and as a matter of fact it should go in the Guinness Book of Records, because the child is able to produce a parent. It is the only thing in the world which reverses the natural order, the child produces the parent. I am speaking of Bell Canada International and Bell Canada Enterprises. The company of Jean de Grandpre makes a billion dollars a year in profit. One sees Mr. de Grandpre on the cover of the Air Canada magazine or other magazines bragging about how he got away from being regulated by the regulators because he was able to spin off another company, and it became a deregulated company.
When we addressed this clause in the clause-by-clause part of the legislative committee, the Minister was asked whether Bell Canada Enterprises-where I talked about the child spinning away the parent, the child being Bell Canada and the parent being Bell Canada Enterprises-was covered by this prohibition. In other words, was Bell Canada Enterprises prohibited from getting into broadcasting? The answer was no. In fact, I believe it was Mr. Palmer of the Minister's Department who said that in response to a question from the Hon. Member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley) who was a member of the committee.
What we are saying with this amendment is that Bell Canada and Bell Canada Enterprises have consistently made efforts to avoid Canadian regulations and regulators by spinning off new companies. Indeed, a Bill was passed by this Government to allow the child, Bell Canada, to give birth to the parent, Bell Canada Enterprises. What we are saying is that this amendment should be perfectly clear and that the prohibition should apply to Bell Canada Enterprises as well as to Bell Canada. The Bell Canada Act, under Amendments to Other Acts states:
Section 7 of the Bell Canada Act is repealed and the following substituted
therefor:
"Neither the company nor any person controlled by the Company shall directly or indirectly hold a licence issued under the Broadcasting Act or carry on a broadcasting undertaking within the meaning of that Act".
We want to amend that to "neither the Company nor its parent, nor any person controlled by the company". Therefore, we make it quite clear that we are talking about Bell Canada and its parent, Bell Canada Enterprises. I think that is the nub of this amendment.
We know how close the Minister is to Bell Canada Enterprises. We remember the famed Saudi caper of recent vintage. That is when the Minister worked hand in hand with Mr. Jean de Grandpre, the President of Bell Canada Enterprises, to end run a CRTC decision. The CRTC had ruled that Bell Canada must use $21 million from overseas operations to cut telephone rates in Canada. The Minister went so far as to write a letter of support for Bell which was used by the company in its appeal to the CRTC. I believe the courts have recently rendered a decision with respect to the Government's continuing interference in this matter. I want to quote Mr. Andrew Roman when, in front of the legislative committee, he said:
"This may sound weird, but 1 would even give consideration to going the other way. What you see under the Broadcasting Act is both broadcasting and cable, and cable is essentially not very different from the telephone companies. While I do not think I would like to have the news brought to you by Bell Canada today in the sense that they are writing the news, I do not see why on the transmission side of it they should not, since they produce fibre optics, coaxial cable, and digitalized network, to be able to provide some competition for the cable companies. But then I have always felt that the hardware delivery side should either be taken right out of the Broadcasting Act or put into a special section and dealt with not as if it were broadcasting. I think it should be dealt with as if it were transmission, which is essentially a hardware and transmission function.
I do not mean by this that it should be dealt with only on the telecom side through the Railway Act, but it should perhaps be left in the Broadcasting Act but dealt with as a separate entity. To the extent that we would not want Bell Canada carrying on the broadcasting activity, I would think that it should cover any associated or affiliated company, yes, because it is so easy to spin off another subsidiary that does the same thing or virtually the same thing under a different label, but when it comes to transmission I would be happy to see them competing with the cable industry because, for one thing, it would bring rates down and for another, it would probably bring quality up."
I do not agree with Mr. Roman's somewhat mischievous suggestion about Bell entering the broadcasting picture. We think that Bell Canada Enterprises and Bell are perhaps even bigger and more powerful than the cable industry, which is already powerful enough. In a short time they could well take over the entire distribution side of broadcasting. We do agree, however, with Mr. Roman and the public interest advocacy group that the distribution undertaking should be dealt with separately and perhaps have similar provisions that apply to Bell in the Railway Act apply to cable companies. I have already offered amendments along these lines which have been voted down by the Government.
September 22, 1988

However, this amendment, if I may just summarize it, makes sure that we catch Bell Canada Enterprises, the parent, that was spun off by that miracle child.

Mr. Speaker, 1 can only support the remarks made by my colleague and suggest to him that based precisely on what he has brought to the attention of this House 1 think perhaps my amendment is a bit fuller in its concept. It covers more, it covers the momma, the poppa, and all the aunts, uncles, sisters, and brothers that might possibly become affiliated. I think the major point here is the fact that cable is a hybrid system. If we were to allow the telcos, particularly Bell Canada, as the first step, into the operations of transmission as a cable system, we would then find them moving into the next step that which we have now accorded to the cable system, and that is as a programmer.
I would like to remind the Minister of her views, which she expressed very succinctly subsequent to my bringing my concerns in this respect to her attention when we were dealing with Bill C-113 on Bell Canada. With respect to Bill C-113, on May 6, 1987, the Minister said that she favoured a preventing of affiliates, not just subsidiaries, of telephone companies from holding broadcast licences. The Minister went further and said: "I believe such a restriction should apply to all federally regulated telephone companies". I would go beyond that and say "all telephone companies", notwithstanding that she went on to say: "We do not tend to favour the telephone company investment in broadcasting receiving undertakings whether directly or affiliated companies".
I recall talking about the child that gave birth to its parents, which is quite a unique undertaking in anyone's world, but it gave birth to a rather unique parent. This parent ended up earning $1 billion profit last year. 1 would say, therefore, it was a very well fed child in the end. Actually, the child who gave birth, Bell Canada, is still a very productive part of the Bell Canada Enterprises. I would suggest that we do not want Bell Canada, Bell Canada affiliates, Bell Canada Enterprises, or any one of them, involved in the broadcast Bill.
The amendment which appears under the Bell Canada Act, through Section 70 of this Act, now prevents Bell Canada only, the regulated monopoly telephone company and its subsidiaries, what flows from the Bell Canada Telephone Company, from holding a broadcast licence. It does not touch Bell Canada Enterprises. I would suggest to the Minister that we would be moving into a very serious situation if we would start with a monopoly transmission facility lending its help and aid to a subsidiary or a sibling or a parent, as the case may be, as one of the affiliates might apply for such a licence.
The potential for conflict must not be permitted. Broadcast and telecommunication policies are not currently advanced enough to allow the entertainment of this particular idea. I would like to suggest that our amendment is valid. The previous Minister of Communications tried such a provision in his first attempt at a Bell reorganization Act under Bill C-19. I would suggest that it was not in the country's interest then and it remains not in the country's interest now. I would strongly recommend the Minister give consideration, through consultation with her own staff, to which one would cover most broadly
Broadcasting Act
either Motion No. 75A of my colleague or my own Motion No. 75B. One or the other, I believe, should be adopted.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to comment briefly on this amendment. The effect of the amendment is to ensure that Bell Canada cannot indirectly, through Bell Canada Enterprises, do what the Bill says it should not do directly, for example, entering into the broadcasting area.
I am surprised the Government would not have accepted this amendment by now, because it has been made quite clear over the course of the past 15 or 20 years that Bell Canada has systematically been seeking to evade regulatory authority of the Government of Canada. It has been aided in so doing by the Liberals when they were in power prior to 1979, again since 1980, and now by the Conservatives in their first full term in office for a very long time.
1 ask myself: What is the reason for that? Why this excessive lassitude when it comes to Bell Canada? Why this complicity with Bell Canada in terms of trying to build it up or allow it to do things which one would have thought the Government agreed it should not do? The only answer I can arrive at is the fact that the Government, be it Liberal or Conservative, has a soft spot for Bell Canada. Of course, I have difficulties with that in a couple of ways. I recognize that Bell runs a more efficient and useful telephone system than many that exist in the world. We benefit from the fact that the telephone system as a whole in North America works pretty well. However, at the same time one must ask whether the cost of that should be to allow continued growth in the nonregulated side which appears to be financed or facilitated by the regulated activity. I think that is a very serious question which the Minister should have taken up.
While I am on my feet, if one wants an example of the problems and corporate irresponsibility which exists, you can look at the situation which is occurring right now. This is a shade distant from the specific purpose of the Bill, but I, as a Member of Parliament, want to register my concern in human terms for the fact that the Bell workers have now been left out on the street for a period of 13 weeks and it looks as though it is going to go on for a lengthy period of time. I want to voice here in the House of Commons my concern for my constituents who have suffered and also for my constituents who are small business people and are suffering because of the deterioration of Bell service. Constituents of mine and other people in this area who are seeking to move into homes or change telephones have also suffered a deterioration of service.
I would like to register my concern for the junior managers who have had to work 60 or 70 hours a week because of the obduracy, obstinacy, and stubbornness with which Bell Canada has continued to hold out against reaching a decent and just settlement with its workers.

September 22, 1988
Broadcasting Act
That is relevant to this particular clause in the sense that this is a company whose primary objective used to be seen as a public service. That does not mean that it was not in the business of making a profit as well. It obviously did. It returned a reasonable stream of dividends and Bell shares were always seen as a safe investment, et cetera. However, a company whose primary objective appeared to be public service seems to have been taken over by an ethic which says that we do not care whether we are in the mortuary business, the telephone business, or anything else, the object of our business, first and foremost, is not to serve our customers, not to look after our employees, not to be good corporate citizens; it is first, last, and foremost just to make a buck, to make as many dollars as we can, and to have the company grow as large as it can.
If that is the guiding principle which is impelling Bell Canada right now, then that means if Bell Canada is prevented from getting into broadcasting, if broadcasting continues to be a lucrative area of endeavour, then Bell Canada will be looking to go indirectly into an area from which it may be barred from going directly. That is why I am suggesting that this amendment, which would ensure that Bell Canada cannot do indirectly what it cannot do directly, should be accepted. I ask the Minister to comment on that when she participates in the debate on this particular section.
1 would also like to have her comment a bit about the human situation of a company which I think is doing itself long-term harm in terms of the way it is handling its labour relations. It is doing a lot of harm to its workers, its customers, its clients, and a lot of small business people across the country when this goes on and on. Surely there must be a more sensible way of running a major enterprise with such an important role in our society, as well as our economy, as Bell Canada has, than to hold out, to keep the last tenth of a per cent out of a wage increase for its employees, to give nickels and dimes only when it comes to a second vote to the point where the employees felt they had no choice after 11 weeks but to reject the company's offer.
There is something wrong with that and I put a lot of the responsibility on Bell management. In acting as they have they have engendered the inquietude and distrust which leads my Party to suggest that this amendment would be appropriate in order to ensure that Bell does not use the back door to get into broadcasting.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to continue my debate on this particular issue brought to our attention by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). I have glad tidings for the Hon. Member. In fact, it is probably more than he deserves after the way he has been treating the Government with respect to child care, the free trade agreement and everything else. However, when we on this side of the House think someone has a good idea, we go along with it.
In a few moments I will be introducing an amendment which will render this private Member's motion acceptable to the Government. It will not change it in any major way but will simply tidy up the wording.
In my previous presentation I said that this is a good idea. There has been all manner of problems in Canada of late, of people making deposits in various deposit-taking institutions not knowing whether or not those deposits were insured under CDIC or being of the assumption that these deposits were insured. In the long run they found out to their chagrin that that was not the case.
It is good fortune for the Hon. Member for Kamloops- Shuswap that he has before us today a motion and not a Bill. On issues such as day care and free trade the Liberals and their good friends the New Democratic Party have been encouraging an attitude of recalcitrance in the Senate. This has flowed over to the ideas put forward by the Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) with respect to heritage railway stations. That Bill has been given a rough ride in the Senate. It is lucky for the Hon. Member that he does not have to go through that route.
I want to make one small comment before going through a prepared presentation. It deals with waiver forms, if we adopted a system of using waivers.
When one goes into a bank or trust company to open an account and puts some money on deposit, one ends up with a whole sheaf of forms, all written in legalese. We are told to sign in the various places marked with an x. If we do not sign, they will not take the money and will not open an account. Very few people read those forms. If there was to be a waiver, it should be in bold print on a separate piece of paper that no one should mistake.
A review of the debate on this motion thus far would show that the House is virtually unanimous in its support for the aims of the Member for Kamloops-Shuswap. As many Members on both sides of the House have pointed out, however, there are a number of problems with the specific proposal which his motion is putting forth.
I agree with several of my colleagues who have indicated that while they support the spirit of the motion, they are unable to support it in its current form because of those shortcomings.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS ADVISABILITY OF INFORMING DEPOSITORS WHEN DEPOSITS ARE UNINSURED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very important proposal. Many Canadians have been caught in a situation where they have placed their deposits in an institution in the belief that in the event the investments of the institution were lost they would have protection for those deposits and would be able to recover those deposits from the institution.
A number of organizations in the early 1980s invested in land. As interest rates escalated and the prices of the land dropped, they were unable to obtain a return on those investments. The depositors in those institutions lost their shirts.
After the smoke and dust had cleared, the people who had put their life savings into these institutions found that there was absolutely no protection for those savings. Had they known this when they first encountered the situation, there certainly would have been some caution and probably another form of investment. I know people who lost virtually their life savings in such organizations. There certainly would have been a great deal more caution in placing their investment, such as by spreading it out into different institutions to protect them from such an occurrence.
We have before us this afternoon an extremely important proposal. I notice in the amendment put forward by the Hon. Member who sits on the government side that the proposal is acceptable and that the Government will support it.
One question I have to ask, however, and it is one which I hope the Government will respond to, is with respect to what seems to be proposed here, although more than acceptable to us because of the action being taken to assist, is that some clarification is needed on how that notice to prospective depositors might come about.
Certainly the fact is that an individual must sit down and have the proposal explained, especially the fact that the deposit is not covered by the Deposit Insurance Corporation and that there is no protection should deposits be lost through investments that do not yield sufficient money to return. We watched the same type of thing happen with the B.C. Teachers Co-op. It is an organization that for many years operated successfully. It accepted deposits from teachers and turned around to pay returns on those deposits. In the final analysis it
got caught in the escalating interest rates and declining land prices and left a great number of its members holding the bag.
Hopefully, the Government will explain the mechanism that it intends to use to have prospective depositors fully informed of the lack of coverage, or the nature of coverage of deposits.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have asked for an opportunity to address the House during this adjournment debate to pursue a question I asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Shields) on July 27. Briefly, I asked if the Government would reconsider the effects on the environment of the Fraser Valley, especially the District of Chilliwack, in making the decision whether or not to reissue the permit to B.C. Hydro for energy exports using the Burrard Thermal Generating Plant.
Although the Parliamentary Secretary replied to my question, I have several points which I would like to highlight, and a couple of questions I wish to raise. First, a quick view of the environment in the Fraser Valley is necessary. The Fraser Valley is one of the world's most productive areas for fish, wildlife and agriculture.
Surrounding the cities of Chilliwack and Abbotsford are rich and abundant crops of raspberries, blueberries, corn, large dairy farms and pastures for raising cattle, sheep and pigs and chicken farms. Farther up the river at Hope and Boston Bar are the forests which make B.C. famous around the world. We are proud of the valley's beauty but, now, we are concerned about its environment and the people who live there.
September 22, 1988

The Burrard Thermal Generating Plant located outside my riding of Fraser Valley East is a 912 megawatt generating station. Unfortunately for us in the valley the prevailing winds from the West which bring the rain to grow our crops also bring nitrogenoxide. Anyone who has done any study on the environment knows that when sulphur and nitrogenoxides combine with water vapour the result is acid rain.
Ozone-not the ozone layer in the upper atmosphere-is a particular reactive form of oxygen that can harm the respiratory system and has been shown to cause leaf damage and reduced crop growth rates. It is produced during warm months when sunlight causes a reaction in the nitrogenoxide and hydrocarbons coming from automobile exhaust and plants. The effects of ozone and acid rain are not new to Canada. I have only to remind the House of the thousands of lakes and forests that are dying in eastern Canada to point out why we are seriously worried about the emission coming from the Burrard Thermal Generating Plant.
We are told that the current air emissions permit for the Burrard generating station will come up for renewal at the end of this year. It will provide for curtailment of operations if ozone levels have reached or are likely to reach 100 on the air quality index. One hundred is the rate of very poor.
Why must we allow the rate to drop so low just to satisfy a clause in a permit? I am sure that I speak on behalf of the mayors and councils of the Chilliwack district and Abbotsford, as well as the residents, when I say that we had better not wait. Our farmers now and our future farmers should not have to suffer for the sake of a permit to export energy.
The long-term health and environmental effects of most of the chemicals now being found in the environment are not known. We do know that some groups of individuals, for example, the elderly, and some specific ecosystems are more susceptible to these contaminants than others.
In 1987 the National Task Force on the Environment and Economy endorsed the replacement of a remedial reactive approach by an anticipate and preventive approach. This is what we should do in the valley.
As I have said already, why should we wait until it is too late? I am pleased that the federal Government has taken a strong stand on environmental issues. We have been the forerunners of some very constructive international environmental measures, such as the Montreal Protocol. We now have the Environmental Protection Act which gives the Canadian Government the necessary authority to implement the Montreal Protocol. This agreement will cut in half by 1999 the emissions of chlorofluorocarbons which seriously affect the global environment. This is good news.
I mentioned that I had some questions. However, I know that time does not allow them to be answered now. First, can the Minister tell us by how much the National Energy Board
Adjournment Debate
has agreed to increase the exports from B.C. Hydro using the Burrard plant? Second, what measures have been taken which would make the people in Chilliwack and the valley aware that steps have been taken to prevent the possible negative effects to the environment from the emissions from the station? A reply at a later date will be appreciated.
My constituents recognize that energy, such as that produced by the Burrard station, is necessary for economic development and social progress, but we are also aware of health and safety issues. Scientific data compiled by the Vancouver Pollution Control Board and the provincial Minister of the Environment show that the plant will send out nitrogen oxides equal to the emissions from a hundred thousand cars annually.
This is a very frightening figure when we think in terms of adding that much pollution to the already polluted air.
Yes, we are concerned. The Burrard Thermal Generating Plant requires our immediate attention. It is not too late to do something about the situation right now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-FRASER VALLEY-EMISSIONS FROM BURRARD THERMAL GENERATING PLANT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to compliment the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Belsher) for his continuing interest in the environmental concerns of those who reside within that region. 1 would also note that the question which he is raising today of course is not only one of considerable consequence, but is also one of very considerable depth. I hope he will appreciate the fact that we may only be able to address some of the points which he has raised in his question.
As you and I both know, and I am sure the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley East knows, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) has a very keen interest in ensuring compatibility between energy and environmental policy. As a result of that, the new electricity policy which was announced a short period ago did address environmental policy.
As a result, we have his commitment and that of the Government to environmental protection. I think we can conclude without too much doubt that the decision by the federal Cabinet to approve the issuance of export permits for electricity from the Burrard Thermal Generating Plant was made only after careful deliberation.
Certainly, the Hon. Member who just spoke is well aware of the history associated with the authorization of exports from this plant. As he knows and as others know, B.C. Hydro applied to the National Energy Board for a licence to export electricity from the province in 1980. The National Energy Board provided approval but excluded exports from this particular thermal plant from the licence.

September 22, 1988
Adjournment Debate
The situation was repeated in 1983, when B.C. Hydro again applied to the board for export licences. Power from the Burrard plant was excluded from the licences because it lacked a pollution control permit, inhibiting the operation of the plant. Since that time, the Burrard station has upgraded its pollution controls and has been granted both a pollution control permit and an energy removal permit or licence from the B.C. regulatory authorities.
B.C. Hydro reapplied to the National Energy Board, seeking approval to use the Burrard station to support electricity exports authorized under the original licences. The National Energy Board and Governor in Council subsequently approved the amendment to the licences.
I would like to stress the following points with reference to the federal authorization of electricity exports from the Burrard station. First of all, the matter has been reviewed not only by the National Energy Board, but also by the Greater Vancouver Regional District and the Environmental Appeal Board of the Province of British Columbia. Each of these agencies, on the basis of evidence studied, has found in favour of permitting B.C. Hydro to operate the Burrard plant.
The waste management permit issued to B.C. Hydro for the operation of the facility restricts pollutant emissions to levels that meet or exceed federal guidelines for emissions from new thermal power generation sources, and B.C. Hydro is committed to reducing its NOx emissions from the plant by an additional 20 per cent.
B.C. Hydro must provide meteorological forecast information to the GVRD for the purpose of assessing air quality conditions whenever the power plant is operated.
The permit furthermore requires B.C. Hydro to advise the district director of the GVRD five days in advance of any planned operation of stations, and gives the director of that agency the authority to curtail operation of the Burrard station when air quality levels of ozone or nitrogen dioxide reach or are predicted to reach specified levels. The specified levels have been set to prevent air quality from reaching the maximum in tolerable levels established by the federal Government for the protection of public health.
Based on these factors, the Government and the Minister are confident that the Burrard Generating Station can be operated without causing air quality in the lower mainland of British Columbia to deteriorate to an unacceptable level.
Furthermore, the waste management permit is up for renewal in December of this year. If circumstances change, and the waste management permit is rescinded or not reissued, the issue will be re-examined at that time and I am sure that the Member for Fraser Valley East will be speaking to the issue at that time.
TRADE-TAX ON LUMBER EXPORTS/IMPORTS OF UNITEDSTATES LUMBER

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-FRASER VALLEY-EMISSIONS FROM BURRARD THERMAL GENERATING PLANT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my application to be heard on the adjournment motion arises out
of a question which 1 directed to the then Minister for International Trade, the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney). It concerns the softwood lumber export tax that was imposed at the behest of the American lobby.
The reason I was dissatisfied with the answer was essentially that the Minister, while providing some information of a more or less relevant type, did not address the gravamen of my question. If I can quote, I asked: "What will the Minister do to attempt to ensure that the tax is not costing Canadian lumber producers Canadian markets?"
This is the major concern in the imposition of the softwood lumber export tax. It would not only reduce Canadian exports to the United States, but by the drastic changes that it involved in the cost of volume equations, it would lead to a much improved ability of American producers to compete in the Canadian market. That prognostication appears to have indeed come true.
I have some recent press reports which I think would be worth citing in terms of that projection. The June 4, 1988 edition of The Globe and Mail records that the President of the Council of Forest Industries of British Columbia, Mr. Apsey, is still calling for Canada to get out of this clause in the softwood lumber tax agreement.
The 15 per cent tax which was imposed on Canadian exports has allowed American producers, now that they have much more secure access to their home market, to increase their production, to drop their marginal cost, and therefore be able to sell into the Canadian market. The lumber tax is not just costing Canadian exports to the United States, but also Canadian shipments to the domestic market.
If I can quote another article on August 27, 1988, also in The Globe and Mail, about a company, Green Forest Lumber Corporation:
One or Canada's leading lumber wholesalers has turned to U.S. wood, U.S.
trains and U.S. dollars to help it stay profitable in difficult economic times.
It goes on to talk about what this company is doing, obviously in response to market forces and the desire, indeed the need, to make a profit, which is taking lumber that it buys in the United States, shipping it across the United States, west to east, and then selling it into the southern Ontario market, which of course is the largest market for construction weights of lumber in the country.
There are a number of other press reports that I can quote of mills shut down because of the 35 per cent tariff on cedar shakes and shingles. We then have the 15 per cent export tax on our softwood lumber exports to the United States.
It appears that we do not have the mechanisms to force the United States to bring, for example, the plywood standards dispute, which is another related and very serious issue, to the Dispute Resolution Tribunal. Under American law they can seek redress before the Federal Trade Commission against the application of that standard which they feel to be discriminatory-
September 22, 1988

The second supplementary question the Minister answered by stating that Canada was selling record amounts of lumber to the domestic market. That is certainly something we would want to look very closely at if we were to accept that statement. The second question was: "What is the Government prepared to do to ensure that we have our share of the Canadian market?"
1 would like to know from the Parliamentary Secretary, who is replying for the Government, what discussions in fact the Government has had with the United States Government regarding this problem of the export tax not only cutting Canadian exports to the United States but, in essence, making the reverse advantage also possible; that is, giving American producers a competitive advantage in selling to Canada.
Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of
Public Works): Mr. Speaker, during Oral Question Period on November 17 last, the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry) directed a question to the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) concerning the export charge on softwood lumber products and alleged increases in imports of U.S. lumber into Canada. In addition, on June 20, the Hon. Member directed a question to the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) concerning a legal action brought against the federal Crown by a group of lumber manufacturing companies, most of which are located in British Columbia. 1 am pleased to respond to the Hon. Member's request for comments on these matters.
The Hon. Member made the allegation in the preamble to his question of November 17 that the sale into Canada of U.S. lumber was de facto dumping and was obviously contrary to the spirit of the free trade agreement. There appears to be considerable confusion in the mind of the hon. gentleman since the case he cites seems to contradict both these statements.
In order for U.S. lumber to be dumped in the Canadian market, it must, by definition, be sold at a price which is lower than the price at which it is offered in the United States market, or sold at less than the cost of production. This is not the claim being made either by the Hon. Member or by the industry spokesmen to whom he referred.
In fact, the Hon. Member stated that the U.S. producers have been able to offer their lumber at competitive prices due to a reduction in their unit costs of production. All of us here would agree that if a company were able to lower its cost of production, it should be allowed to benefit from this achievement in the international market-place without undue restriction.
Adjournment Debate
Canadians have always been able to purchase U.S. lumber on the open market and there have always been imports of U.S. lumber into Canada. These have been traditionally much smaller than the Canadian exports of lumber to the United States, but imports from the U.S.A. are not uncommon. The fact that these took place after the imposition of the export charge on softwood lumber products does not imply in any way that the U.S. products were dumped, and certainly not that the spirit of the Canada-U.S. free trade deal was thwarted.
Canadian exports to the U.S.A. have declined slightly, but this has been more than offset by growth in both the Canadian and other export markets. I note particularly that the Japanese market has taken much more of our lumber than it has in past years. The growth in exports and the buoyant domestic market in Canada have resulted in an over-all increase in Canadian production of softwood lumber in 1987 over a year earlier. While the 1988 market is off somewhat, the current high levels of production point to another reasonable year for the industry.
In summary, no evidence has been presented that Canadian producers are losing a share of the Canadian market due to unfairly traded U.S. lumber. On the subject of the legal action brought against the Crown, it would not be appropriate for me to comment directly on the issues now before the courts.
1 would like to comment briefly, however, on the agreement which is the basis for the questions the Hon. Member has raised. It is worth recalling that Canada entered into the Memorandum of Understanding as a means to resolve a major trade dispute with the United States and to avoid the imposition by the U.S. of a countervailing duty on our softwood lumber exports. As a result, provinces have retained the flexibility they need to make changes in their forest management policies. Revenues which would have otherwise gone to the U.S. Treasury remain in Canada. In the first year the export tax was in place, this represented approximately $400 million. This has been distributed to the provinces.
Moreover, all lumber produced in B.C. is exempt from the export charge following implementation of replacement measures by that province, and the charge has been reduced from 15 per cent to 8 per cent for exports from Quebec, the second largest producing province, again on the basis of replacement measures. In fact, most of the softwood lumber exports are now exempt from the export charge.
